#2694. Why a long-term mega deal for Tarik Skubal isn't actually all that risky

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The big prize of this free agent class is ace lefty and two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal. We've seen and will continue to see predictions that he's going to land a deal of around 8-10 years and topping $400 million. The knee-jerk reaction to such prognostications in many corners will be that he won't possibly be "worth" that much and that such a deal would be a huge "risk" to the signing team.

Let's stop right there. I don't think it's all that risky. There's risk for the team on every contract, especially pitchers, of course, but in Skubal, the signing team is getting a surefire ace for several years.

Let's examine some of the reasons why such an enormous deal isn't actually that dangerous.

Since returning from surgery in 2023, Skubal has been absurdly good. Across his ages 26-29 seasons, he's made 103 starts and has gone 50-20 with a 2.47 ERA (169 ERA+), 0.92 WHIP and 757 strikeouts in 626 ⅓ innings. He's only walked 109, or 1.6 per nine innings. He rarely gets hit hard, he rarely gives up many runs, he strikes out a high number of hitters and rarely walks any. Simply, he's been good at everything.

The recent track record here says this is the best pitcher in baseball, at least in the long view (we could argue Paul Skenes was better in 2025 and Jacob Misiorowski was better in 2026, to name two examples, but if we looked at 2023-present, it isn't all that close).

There isn't a dropoff in the postseason, either. In eight playoff starts, Skubal has a 2.13 ERA, 0.79 WHIP and 70 strikeouts against nine unintentional walks in 50 ⅔ innings.

Also, the career workload isn't anything to be concerned about. Skubal heads to his age-30 season now with only 925 ⅓ innings in the regular season. Even counting the playoffs doesn't get Skubal to 1,000 innings at the big-league level. Let's go back to Skenes. He's only 24 years old and already has 495 career innings. Another ace? Justin Verlander had 1,553 ⅔ career innings through his age-29 season.

There just isn't a ton of tread on these Skubal tires.

We'll hear plenty of consternation about Skubal being 30 years old next season as it relates to signing a long-term deal. We'll also hear people say a deal is risky due to his injury history. He had Tommy John surgery in college, flexor tendon surgery in 2022 and arthroscopic surgery (a new procedure using a Nanoscope) in 2026.

The simple matter is that pretty much every pitcher nowadays has had some sort of surgery on his arm, notably the elbow, and we've seen pitchers time and again bounce back after elbow surgery to perform at a high level.

Skubal just did it. He only missed roughly six weeks after his procedure this past season. He came back to make 19 starts after the surgery and posted a 2.73 ERA with 141 strikeouts in 115 ⅓ innings.

I mentioned Verlander above. Skubal is a multi-time Cy Young winner, so it's acceptable to look at some of the best pitchers in baseball and how they aged into their late-30s in recent memory.

Again, Skubal will be in his age-30 season in 2027. If he signs an eight-year deal, it'll run through his age-37 season.

For those so worried about the long-term finances of the team owner who ends up signing Skubal, are you sure you're really worried that he won't be productive through five, six, seven or even all eight years of that deal? Given his track record, talent, pitching arsenal, relatively low workload given his age and how well some of the best pitchers have fared through their mid-30s, he actually seems like a great bet.

A decade ago, the common talking point was that long and huge deals for pitchers never age well. That isn't actually the case, for the most part. Here are some of the biggest pitcher contracts of all time and how they unfolded (or are unfolding).

Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Dodgers, 12 years, $325 million -- He came over from Japan for his age-25 season, so this one was a different animal. Still, it sure doesn't seem like it'll be a bad deal, does it?

Gerrit Cole, Yankees, 9 years, $324 million -- Through six years of the deal, Cole has missed a chunk of time due to Tommy John surgery. He's also won a Cy Young, finished top four in Cy Young voting three times, been worth 22.4 WAR and was the ace of an American League pennant winner.

Stephen Strasburg, Nationals, 7 years, $245 million -- Here's the bust. Strasburg was never healthy again after the 2019 World Series title run. Still, the Nationals wouldn't have that title without him.

Justin Verlander, Tigers, 10 years, $219.5 million -- This was the deal that ran from 2010-19. During this deal, Verlander won two Cy Youngs (one in the second year of the deal, one in the final year), a World Series, three pennants, 160 games and led the league in pitcher WAR three times.

Max Fried, Yankees, 8 years, $218 million -- It's only been two years, but Fried is 24-10 with a 2.83 ERA and finished fourth in AL Cy Young voting in his first year.

David Price, Red Sox, 7 years, $217 million -- He won a World Series in the third year of the contract. Overall, he was 53-26 with a 3.78 ERA (118 ERA+) through the course of the deal.

Corbin Burnes, Diamondbacks, 6 years, $210 million -- Burnes had his first year of the deal interrupted by Tommy John surgery. He had a 2.66 ERA through 11 starts prior to the injury. The jury's still out, but he heads to his age-32 season fully recovered now.

Zack Greinke, 6 years, $206.5 million -- Over the course of this deal, Greinke was 77-39 with a 3.55 ERA (125 ERA+) and 19.9 WAR. He had a fourth-place Cy Young finish in there.

CC Sabathia, 9 years, $202 million -- The Yankees won the World Series in Sabathia's first year there and he started the deal with three straight top-four Cy Young finishes. Overall, during this deal, he was 120-73 with 27.1 WAR and had five straight 200-plus inning seasons.

Max Scherzer, 7 years, $191.4 million -- During this contract, Scherzer won two Cy Youngs, a World Series title and 99 games with a 2.75 ERA. He posted 41.8 WAR. In the seven years on this deal, Scherzer finished in the top five in Cy Young voting six times, with 2020 being the outlier.

We can close with this. Some people might not care for such a measure, particularly the salary cap crowd who will be worried about the owners paying too much. Regardless, let's stick with the general belief that each individual WAR (1.0 WAR) is worth a bit over $8 million per season.

By this measure, Skubal was worth $48.4 million in 2024, $53.7 million in 2025 and $41.7 million last season. Putting aside how much less money he actually made than what he was doing on the field, and knowing everything laid out above, I'll ask a simple question:

Are you sure a 10-year, $400 million deal for this guy would be a "risk?"

I think we could argue that it would be a bargain.

#2693. Mikal Bridges buzzer-beater, Victor Wembanyama monster stats highlight NBA action

There were six NBA games on Saturday, Nov. 21, which is a lighter schedule for the 30-team league.

But fewer games did not mean a shortage of action. Stars across the country had impressive nights, from career-highs to a thrilling buzzer-beater.

Victor Wembanyama had a monster night by scoring 50 points as the anchor of an incredibly rare statline to keep the San Antonio Spurs' momentum strong.

Tyler Herro also scored 50 points, which was the Milwaukee Bucks star's career-high.

Elsewhere, Mikal Bridges wowed with a buzzer-beater to give the New York Knicks their fourth straight win.

Here's a breakdown of the NBA highlights from the day:

Wembanyama proved why his nickname is the Alien in the Spurs' 114-91 win over the New Orleans Pelicans. The San Antonio big man posted 50 points, 19 rebounds, four steals and five blocks in the effort.

According to the NBA, Wembanyama is the first player since the 1973-74 season to notch 50 points, at least 15 boards, four steals and five blocks in one game. ESPN adds that he is the first player in league history to have 50 points, five blocks and five made 3-point shots in a single matchup.

He is also the third San Antonio player to record multiple 50-point games in the same season. He had 52 points and 24 rebounds earlier this month in a win over the Dallas Mavericks.

The Spurs have won 14 of their last 15 games and had a 12-game winning streak that was broken earlier in the week.

The national hype might be around Herro's former team, the Miami Heat, with the release of "Grand Theft Auto 6." But the Bucks guard made basketball fans pay attention to him when he scored a career-high 50 points. He added 11 rebounds and almost scored the game-tying 3-point bucket, but his shot was milliseconds too late and the Bucks lost to LeBron James and the Philadelphia 76ers 132-129.

According to the Bucks, Herro, who joined the Heat in the Giannis Antetokounmpo trade, is the first player in NBA history to have at least 50 points, 11 boards, seven 3-point shots, and shoot 65% from the field in a single game.

Joel Embiid led the 76ers with 26 points, 17 rebounds and nine assists.

Mikal Bridges wowed by scoring the game-winning shot for the Knicks at the buzzer.

With 3.2 seconds left, he took the inbound from Josh Hart, dribbled and took a side step in front of Portland Trail Blazers forward Toumani Camara and then launched a shot from behind the arc that drained the net smoothly.

The Knicks beat the Trail Blazers 97-96 after Portland came back from a 26-point deficit. Bridges finished with 12 points and Finals MVP Jalen Brunson led New York with 30 points and seven rebounds.

Georgia took care of business against South Carolina on Saturday.

The win improved the Bulldogs to 10-1 overall and clinched their spot in the SEC Championship Game. They also made history, becoming the first team in SEC history to make six straight SEC Championship Games.

#2690. Fantasy Football Rankings: Hayden Winks' WR Blueprint for Week 11

The Blueprint is my weekly column and basically everything that I use to build out the most accurate rankings I can. There will be an RB column, this WR column and a combination column on the onesie positions. You will find film notes and endless charts. Maybe enough charts to stress test the Yahoo website. I kid.

It's impossible to get every ranking thoroughly early in the week, so be sure to keep checking in on these columns through Sunday morning. As always, my full rankings at every position are available.

1. Ja'Marr Chase (at WAS) - 94.5 proj. receiving yards

Chase is back to averaging 98 YPG this year after a WR1 overall stretch over the past month. The Commanders are a pass-funnel defense without a strong secondary. They've allowed the fifth-most passing YPG, and Chase hung 118-2 against them in his only game against Washington back in 2024.

2. CeeDee Lamb (vs. TEN) - 90.5 proj. receiving yards

Lamb has been pretty up-and-down this year, but on average, he's the WR3 on WR2 overall usage as a no-doubt Round 1 value. He's leading the position in target share (39%) and air yards (145) over the past month, as the Cowboys defense has continued to allow anyone through the front door.

Now he gets a dream matchup against a Titans defense allowing 35.0 half PPR points per game to WRs (first). They've allowed the most points under 20 air yards, specifically, where Lamb does almost all of his damage. They've been even worse of late without DT Jeffery Simmons and S Amani Hooker. Dallas enters as 8.5-point home favorites with a slate-leading 31.5-point team total (first).

3. Justin Jefferson (at SF) - 84.5 proj. receiving yards

The Vikings passed more in neutral situations last week with Kirk Cousins compared to over the past year and a half with underwhelming QBs. That'll help Jefferson find his mid-range WR1 groove, on top of those throws being far more accurate. Jefferson had three screens last week, plus other underneath targets, allowing him to post a season-high 19.3 expected half PPR points (WR5). They didn't rip the explosive play, but those will be coming. In the short term, Jordan Addison won't be out there either.

This week is a great spot for Jefferson. The Vikings are slight dogs, yet still have a 21.5-point team total in what should be a down week across the NFL. The 49ers were shredded by the Cowboys' pass game last week and have been given up 27.7 half PPR points to WR rooms on average this entire season. Most of those will go to Jefferson here.

4. Amon-Ra St. Brown (vs. TB) - 81.5 proj. receiving yards

St. Brown was on a five-game streak without a touchdown before finishing last week with 23.8 half PPR points in Germany with a couple of long scores. He's been a target monster all year long and remains a positive regression candidate. The slot star is the WR5 on WR4 usage and WR4 targets per game this year.

The Buccaneers have been stout against WRs overall, ranking 24th in half PPR points allowed (24.1 per game). However, they rank seventh in points allowed to receiver targets under 10 air yards, fitting St. Brown's underneath profile. Big slots like Luther Burden III (WR9) and Germie Bernard (WR6) have had spike weeks against them recently. Detroit enters as seven-point home favorites with a 25.25-point team total (ninth).

5. Tee Higgins (at WAS) - 74.5 proj. receiving yards

It'll be hard to run as pure as he has so far. Higgins is the WR6 on WR16 usage and WR14 targets per game. The good news is Higgins has the best film of his career, and Joe Burrow is firmly in his absolute prime. This is a pairing that should be dunking all over models. On top of that, the Bengals have the highest neutral pass rate (67%) in the NFL. When games are close, Higgins will see eight+ targets per game. The Commanders are an eruption spot.

6. Nico Collins (vs. IND) - 71.5 proj. receiving yards

Collins ran more routes last week — thank you!!! — and it worked. He turned 15 targets into a WR7 week. The Browns held their own in the second half by blitzing and playing tight man coverage behind it. Collins will have more space to operate in future matchups, and the Texans offense is trending towards being more and more pass-heavy. They're now fifth in neutral pass rate after usually being bottom-10 under the DeMeco Ryans regime. Collins is a fringe WR1/2 with plenty of weekly upside.

Collins is looking to extend his four-game streak of 100+ yards against Indy. The Colts won't have CB1 Sauce Gardner, nor CB2 Charvarius Ward. This should be BBQ chicken. Houston enters as 12.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 28.5 points (fifth).

7. George Pickens (vs. TEN) - 69.5 proj. receiving yards

We're so back. Pickens is the WR12 on WR10 usage this season, on WR11 targets per game. He's not even running hot either. He finally had one of his signature blowup games last week, thanks to the Cowboys' unwatchable defense. Pickens is on the WR1/2 border depending on the matchup. He is best when facing single high, as Dak Prescott can take perimeter shots to him with more success.

The Titans don't have anyone in the secondary to worry about. They've allowed the most fantasy points to WRs, including the third-most points on targets with 15+ air yards. They won't have FS Amani Hooker roaming deep now either. Dallas carries a 31.5-point implied team total (first) as 8.5-point home favorites.

8. Zay Flowers (at CAR) - 68.5 proj. receiving yards

It would've been best if Lamar Jackson was playing like the MVP, but PPR scam artist Jacoby Brissett is a great backup plan for Flowers' fantasy appeal. We instantly felt that last week when they trailed the Chargers. They had a season-high neutral pass rate (73%) in an offense that's been last in dropbacks per game since 2022 when Flowers entered the NFL. We'll trade some downfield completions for more volume moving forward. I'm throwing out the Week 8-9 sample and putting more faith into last week's 6-74-0 line on seven targets.

We'll see if the Panthers are still going to be without their top-2 CBs later in the week. They've been middle of the pack against fantasy WRs this year, with Jordyn Tyson turning 13 targets into 80 scoreless yards last week as the most recent example.

9. Parker Washington (at NYG) - 67.5 proj. receiving yards

Washington can get game-scripted out of production in second halves, but that is a good problem to have, as he can either go crazy early or walk into full-game production when games are tighter. He's inside the top 15 in every per-route metric essentially, and Washington is still the WR13 despite being the WR25 in targets per game. It's clear that he's both Trevor Lawrence and Liam Coen's favorite target. How could he not be? He's smart, physical, explosive and can be used inside and out. Star.

The Giants do have a strong secondary with a great CB1 in Deonte Banks. Washington gets moved around into favorable matchups, and I trust Coen to find spots for him. But the Giants are 30th in passing yards per game allowed (196). They've shut down deep targets in particular, so it's possible Washington racks up more underneath and intermediate targets this time around. Jacksonville travels as 6-point road favorites with a 26.25-point team total (seventh).

10. Malik Nabers (vs. JAX) - 69.5 proj. receiving yards

Nabers is the WR12 on WR4 overall usage since Week 5 after knocking off the rust early. He's still not 100% himself and does seem to be mad offline, but the spike-week potential is fully on the menu when the ball is going his way. Over that span, only JSN, Puka Nacua, Ja'Marr Chase and Justin Jefferson are ahead of him in target share, so when the Giants are forced into dropbacks, expect huge games down the stretch. J.J. McCarthy is pushing the ball on these deeper out routes relentlessly and looks generally improved, even if he's volatile.

The Jaguars will be a real test. Travis Hunter is in the mix for the second-best CB tape right now, and he'll be joined by FS Jessie Bates III now. The only good news is the Giants are expected to be trailing, and offenses facing the Jaguars have the second-highest neutral pass rate (59%). For those reasons, the Jaguars are 15th in fantasy points allowed to WRs. The Giants enter as 6-point home underdogs carrying an implied team total of 20.25 points (18th).

11. Luther Burden III (vs. NO) - 59.5 proj. receiving yards

12. Garrett Wilson (at LAC) - 65.5 proj. receiving yards

Update: Omar Cooper Jr. and Isaiah Williams are both out, so the Jets' starting and backup slot receivers are out. Perhaps the Jets use Wilson in more creative ways this week and at the very least there is slightly easier target competition, though one pivot would be to increase first-round TE Kenyon Sadiq's snaps. Wilson is the WR20 on WR14 usage this season.

The Chargers defense has been one of the friendliest environments for WRs, ranking 5th in half PPR points allowed to the position. Opposing passing attacks facing Los Angeles have passed at a 57% neutral clip (5th-highest in the NFL), funneling volume into a secondary that just surrendered 26.5 points to Kayshon Boutte and 18.5 points to Tank Dell in Week 9. The Jets will look to exploit that vulnerability as 3.5-point road underdogs with an implied total of 19 points (19th).

13. Carnell Tate (at DAL) - 65.5 proj. receiving yards

Tate (shoulder) has been limited in practice after missing the last handful of games. This assumes he's ready to role, while Wan'Dale Robinson was placed on IR and Calvin Ridley was demoted. It'll be Tate, Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike in 3-WR sets moving forward. That's not much of a competition for Tate, who has lived up to his NFL draft status to me. He can win on breaking routes and has great hands. His skill set stands to benefit with the changes the Titans have made offensively with Tate banged up:

Over his past 4 games, Tate is the WR25 on WR22 usage and WR20 targets per game. In good matchups, he can be viewed as a boom-bust WR2 now. The Cowboys are a great matchup. They've allowed the 6th-most fantasy points to WRs, while struggling to defend Keenan Allen and Deebo Samuel last week as the latest example. Michael Wilson is the closest real life comp to Tate, and he hung 128-1 on them as the WR4 three games ago. Tennessee owns a 23.0-point team total this week, easily their highest of the season.

14. DJ Moore (vs. MIA) - 47.5 proj. receiving yards

I wrote about DJ Moore in my weekly film review series.

This week, the Bills catch an injured, inexperienced Dolphins defense at home with a monster 31.0-point team total. The upside is obvious. He just has to come down with one of his downfield shots.

15. Chris Olave (at CHI) - 68.5 proj. receiving yards

I wrote about Olave's potential role change in last week's film review column, but long story short is Tyson is an underneath and intermediate player who is taking away snaps from vertical-threat Bryce Lance. Olave inherited some of the Lance clear out route role last week, to the point that he had season lows in all metrics. The Saints would be in a worse spot if that continued, but that is the risk in the short term as we learn more. Olave is simply too good to go away in an offense that's first in neutral pace with a struggling defense. The more likely scenario that emerges is he takes a volume haircut and settles in as a more volatile WR2, while Tyson dances near the line of scrimmage.

The good news is the Bears have struggled specifically against the Olave skill set. They've allowed the sixth-most fantasy points on 15+ air yard throws to WRs, while nickel CB Kyler Gordon has helped sure up throws under 10 air yards where the Bears have allowed the fewest points per game. Getting over the top is the only hope the Saints have of making this a game. New Orleans heads to Chicago as 11.5-point road underdogs with an implied total of 18.5 points (20th).

16. Jordyn Tyson (at CHI) - 56.5 proj. receiving yards

I wrote about Tyson in the film review once again. Check that out.

This week's matchup against the Bears has some positives and negatives. The negatives are the Saints only project for 18.5 points and may struggle getting onto the field against a clock-killing offense. Their best defensive back is also slot CB Kyler Gordon, who has the exact skill set that could give an in-development rookie some issues. That said, the Saints can get into crazy dropback environments as the fastest-paced offense when trailing. They're 11.5-point dogs this time around, so it's not hard to see both Saints WRs with 10ish targets here. In a closer game last week, Tyson had 13 of them. When in doubt, lean into the volume.

17. Tetairoa McMillan (vs. BAL) - 63.5 proj. receiving yards

McMillan is averaging 8.2 half PPR points on 11.7 expected points in his eight games with Jalen Coker this year. Over the past month against a more difficult schedule, he's the WR53 on WR25 usage. He hasn't been getting as open of late, and then Bryce Young has missed him up the sideline a bit too often. He's still handling 24% targets in an offense that leans pass first in neutral situations, but the alpha WR1 traits haven't fully blossomed in his second season. He's a very good, not elite, WR to me.

The Ravens sent home podcaster Marlon Humphrey, not that he was very good in coverage this year. He'll battle with CB1 Nate Wiggins, who is much lighter but much faster than McMillan. There will be some 50/50 balls that he needs to come down with to win this individual matchup. Tre' Harris (WR24), Parker Washington (WR19), D.J. Moore (WR13) and Tee Higgins (WR2) were able to do just that this past month against them. The Panthers are 2.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 23.5 points (12th).

18. Rashee Rice (vs. ARI) - 50.5 proj. receiving yards

Rice is the WR25 on WR43 usage this season, removing his injured game in Week 4. He hasn't had a better finish than WR12 in a week, as the offense has become more balanced in all phases including the red zone. They've also split up the underneath WR role between he and Xavier Worthy, and now Josh Downs is in the intermediate mix. The role tweaks have been a lid on his fantasy value, but the Chiefs are also back to being one of the best offenses in the NFL. There will be spike weeks coming as a boom-bust WR2.

The Cardinals defense enters Week 11 ranked 12th in half PPR points allowed to opposing WR rooms. Arizona's secondary has allowed production to the Rice zone, sitting seventh in points allowed to WRs on throws between 5-20 yards downfield. The Chiefs are 15.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 28.5 points (sixth).

19. Stefon Diggs (vs. CIN) - 46.5 proj. receiving yards

Diggs is quietly the WR21 on WR24 usage this season and could hold the line with Terry McLaurin out for the season. He's not a full-time player, nor as quick as he once was, but his game ages gracefully as a crafty player with excellent hands and toughness. Diggs has been manufactured some targets on top of being their most relied upon underneath and intermediate target.

This is an excellent spot for him with the Bengals expected to put a beating on the Commanders' defense. Game script should be on his side, and he needs these 3-WR sets to get onto the field. On top of that, the Bengals have a fantastic CB1 in D.J. Turner on the perimeter, but Diggs will avoid him and settle into where Cincy has been the worst at defending: the middle. Similar WRs like Chimere Dike (WR8) and Zay Flowers (WR3) have had great games against them recently, while traditional WR1s have struggled. The Commanders project for 23.75 points (11th), too.

20. Jaylen Waddle (vs. LV) - 42.5 proj. receiving yards

Waddle (concussion) has been a full participant and hopefully will be able to finish this next game after injuries have piled up. Waddle only has one game above 13.5 half PPR points this season, and his 5.8 targets per game sit far lower than most, including myself, expected. They had the bye week to figure out how to feature him more, and it's possible he's one of the few veteran WRs who get better down the stretch. That's at least the hope with Bo Nix playing better later in the season than early on historically.

The real hope sits with the matchup. The Raiders have allowed the most yards to WRs in the slot this season on the highest QBR. Against all fantasy WRs, the Raiders have allowed the seventh-most fantasy points, including a blow up game against JSN (WR3). The Broncos have a 25.5-point team total (ninth) at home. Please come through.

21. Emeka Egbuka (at DET) - 45.5 proj. receiving yards

Egbuka has been more good than great on tape this year. He battled a toe injury in training camp and then has picked up new injuries along the way. Baker Mayfield said he "looks great right now" after hinting that the injuries have prevented him from taking off earlier this year. For what it's worth, Egbuka is not on the injury report at all right now and that was not the case earlier this year.

Across the entire season, Egbuka is the WR33 on WR19 usage. Those are probably closer to his floor. We'll see if the Bucs going to more Tez Johnson forced Eguka to play outside more, but to put things simply, the Buccaneers are desperate for Egbuka to turn into an alpha. Everyone else doesn't have the skills to do that, and the pass game has been unwatchable. I can argue he is still frequently the designed first read on a bulk of the Bucs' dropbacks. Everyone has to just play better.

The Lions are too injured at all three levels to be nervous about the matchup. The Bucs are unlikely to be in full run the clock out mode like they've been in the past, and we'll see if CB1 D.J. Reed (hip) can suit up. There should be time for whoever is starting at QB to deliver the ball with Aidan Hutchinson out. A lowly 18.25-point team total holds expectations in check. We're chasing volume more than anything.

22. DeVonta Smith (vs. PIT) - 53.5 proj. receiving yards

Smith is expected to return after a pair of injuries have derailed his 2026 season. Since 2025, Smith is the WR21 on WR25 usage. While he doesn't have A.J. Brown to compete with, he also plays in a bottom-5 offense now. It's hard to calibrate all of the moving pieces, so Smith is a boom-bust WR3 until we have a better clue for how Joe Milton is going to fit in with Smith.

On top of that, the Steelers have an excellent DL that can spoil the entire game. Philly only has a 17.5-point team total, and I totally get it.

23. Rome Odunze (vs. NO) - 45.5 proj. receiving yards

Odunze is the WR33 on WR41 usage since Caleb Williams returned in Week 6. He's not going to get the manufactured touches like others in the offense, and there are games that are taken over by the ground attack. Odunze will have to make good on his red zone and downfield targets to pay off as an upside WR3 in fantasy. That has been an issue for him for too long, but he's very much due for more long scores as we've outlined in this column before he finished as the WR13 (4-60-1) in Week 9.

The matchup suits Odunze well. The Saints have allowed the fifth-most points to WRs on throws over 15 air yards, while being quite good on intermediate and underneath throws. On top of that, S Justin Reid just asked for his release. A 30.0-point team total for Chicago is the invitation for WR2/3 hope.

24. Mike Evans (vs. MIN) - 47.5 proj. receiving yards

Evans (achilles tendinitis) went DNP-limited-limited in practice but is on track to play per his agent and the national insiders. It's a workload-based injury, and this is an important game for seeding in the NFC picture, so it makes sense for them to push his return. It'd also make sense to not push him to anywhere near 100% snaps. I'm projecting him for a part-time yet effective role against the league's best (and most unique) defense. Evans has a 66-1 game against Brian Flores back in 2023, but that defense wasn't nearly as polished as this one.

The 49ers also have the altitude to worry about in Mexico City, so there are far more unusual things to factor in, none of them working in his favor. While playing through various ailments this year, Evans is the WR17 on WR21 usage. Knocking him a tier below that feels fair to me. He's a boom-bust WR3 with six teams on bye.

25. Jalen Coker (vs. BAL) - 42.5 proj. receiving yards

Coker's output has dried up over the past month. Across his last four games, he is the WR87 in half PPR points per game on WR59 expected-points usage, averaging just 1.8 receptions on 4.0 targets. His target share has sat right around 13% across that stretch, bottoming out in Week 10 with 0 catches on four targets against New Orleans. That is a noticeable step back from his full-season baseline, where he sits as the WR32 on WR30 usage while logging 6.3 targets per contest.

The Ravens provide a middle-of-the-road matchup, ranking 16th in half PPR points allowed per game to opposing wide receivers. Baltimore has been much more vulnerable to intermediate targets, where they rank 10th in points allowed, than underneath throws where they rank 26th. While Tee Higgins posted 148 yards and a touchdown against them in Week 7, Quentin Johnston was held to just six yards on one target in Week 10. Carolina enters as 2.5-point home favorites with an implied team total of 23.5 points (12th).

26. Jameson Williams (vs. TB) - 50.5 proj. receiving yards

Never get too high or too low on Jamo. He's a boom-bust WR22 just about every season now. This year, Williams is the WR25 on WR31 usage with stretches of WR1 and WR4 play.

This is a matchup to be more concerned with. The Bucs have two great CBs, and Zyon McCollum is just as good of an athlete as Williams is. That's partially why the Bucs have allowed the fourth-fewest fantasy points to WRs on 15+ air yard throws this year. Tampa Bay is a pass funnel defense, but a lot of that is in the Amon-Ra St. Brown and Sam LaPorta zone. It doesn't mean that Williams can't take it to the crib on low volume, but there have been better matchups per-game than this one. The Lions still have a 25.25-point team total (ninth).

27. DK Metcalf (at PHI) - 42.5 proj. receiving yards

Update: Michael Pittman Jr. (foot) won't play, but Roman Wilson will enter into the lineup here. At the same time, the Eagles placed LB Zack Baun on IR and aren't the scary defense we're used to. The Steelers should win this game here, but Metcalf will go to work against star CB1 Quinyon Mitchell, while the offense has turned away from the pass game in recent weeks with both running backs healthy. He's a positive regression candidate but the time of him being a true No. 1 receiver has came and gone. He's the WR38 on WR20 usage this year. Splitting the gap is fair.

28. Caleb Douglas (at BUF) - 48.5 proj. receiving yards

Chrisitan Benford (groin) hasn't practiced, but the Bills added S Amani Hooker at the deadline and have a more menacing DL in 2026. It'll be almost entirely zone defense for Douglas to sort through with an inexperienced QB. It'll be a tough spot. To his credit, Douglas has been the WR22 on WR50 usage since returning from injury. He's a boom-bust WR3/4 with better odds of flaming out here.

29. Ladd McConkey (vs. NYJ) - 40.5 proj. receiving yards

McConkey rug pulled in Week 9 and then missed Week 10 with back spasms. He's back to limited practices this week. We'll learn more later. #2689. MLB rumors: Phillies OF on the trading block, Blue Jays eye ex-Yankee, plus Mets, Mariners, Braves, Rays, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Thursday marks the final day of the General Manager meetings in Las Vegas. Though we haven't seen any major moves this offseason, we have seen an uptick in rumors in the past few days and that isn't a coincidence. Put a bunch of reporters and front-office execs in the same area for three or four days and chatter picks up, even if there isn't a ton of actual substance behind it.

Rumors are always fun, so let's round up the latest right here in addition to any news.

We have one of our first major-league deals of the offseason as the Braves have signed reliever Evan Phillips to a three-year, $35 million deal. Phillips ranked No. 34 on our top 50 free agent list.

Phillips, a 32-year-old right-hander, has been a setup man or closer for the Dodgers for the last several seasons. In returning from surgery last season, he appeared in 31 games, pitching to a 3.46 ERA and 1.07 WHIP with 33 strikeouts in 26 innings. The majority of his closing experience came in 2023 when he had 24 saves in 27 chances.

The Braves' closer last season was Raisel Iglesias, but he's a free agent. Holdover Robert Suarez could take over those duties while Phillips, lefty Dylan Lee and youngster Didier Fuentes are also in the late-inning mix.

The Blue Jays went from one of the best offensive teams in 2025 to one of the worst in 2026. They'd love a big bounceback from Vladimir Guerrero Jr., among other positive movements, but they also look for outside help. Might that help come in the form of free agent infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr.?

The Jays have met with representatives for Chisholm, reports Sportsnet.

Chisholm, 28, hit .231/.312/.399 last season, but had a huge 2025 and any signing team would be hoping for the 2025 version of Chisholm.

The Jays do have a capable incumbent second baseman in Ernie Clement, but either Clement or Chisholm can be used in the outfield and the Blue Jays certainly need outfield upgrades.

The Phillies have been telling opposing teams that they are not "locked into anything" regarding their current outfield situation, according to The Athletic, so much so that All-Star outfielder Brandon Marsh is available in a trade.

As things stand, with Bryce Harper moving back to first base, the Phillies would have Bryan De La Cruz in right, Justin Crawford in center and Marsh in left, but that all seems pretty fluid as they look to upgrade the ballclub and keep that window of contention open.

Marsh, 28, had a stellar start last season, leading to his first-ever All-Star Game. Through July 1, he hit .319/.352/.530. The rest of the way, however, he slashed .177/.241/.241, dragging him down overall to a 90 OPS+ and 0.4 WAR on the season.

The Mariners have shown interest in free agent left fielder Ian Happ, per MLB Network.

Happ, 32, has spent his entire 10-year MLB career with the Cubs, who drafted him in the first round all the way back in 2015. He was pretty consistent from 2022-25, averaging 3.9 WAR with a .251/.347/.433 (118 OPS+) line and winning four Gold Gloves. Last season, though, he dipped to .218/.326/.412 (103 OPS+) with 2.7 WAR. He still topped 20 home runs for the fifth time in the last six years.

The Mariners have a vacancy in left field with Randy Arozarena having hit free agency and a need to upgrade their offense.

Yesterday's big news was the Yankees' interest in free agent first/third baseman Alec Bohm and The Athletic reports that we can now add the Mets to the list of suitors.

Bohm hit .249/.315/.383 (87 OPS+) with 15 home runs, 88 RBI and -0.2 WAR last season. It might be surprising to see him garnering such interest on the open market, but there isn't much right-handed power out there and Bohm finished last season strong (.318/.402/.453 in his last 42 games). The Mets, meanwhile, are desperate for help at the cold corner after last year's disastrous Jorge Polanco experiment. Jared Young did provide a glimmer of hope at first base before suffering a concussion in September while colliding with a teammate on a play.

Free agent starting pitcher Dustin May has a decent market right now, according to MLB Network, with at least the Cubs, White Sox, Padres and Astros having shown interest in the right-hander.

May, 29, made 31 starts between the Cardinals and Brewers last season, going 7-9 with a 4.70 ERA in 145 ⅔ innings. He showed flashes of brilliance with the Cardinals and had a stretch from April 10 to June 15 during which he posted a 2.54 ERA in 12 starts, but in the end there was plenty of inconsistency and even bad, forcing him into a bullpen role in the playoffs for the champion Brewers.

Free agent catcher Ryan Jeffers has been extended the qualifying offer from the Twins, meaning he has to decide by net Tuesday whether to accept the one-year, $23.15 million contract or hit free agency. There's nothing that says a team can't re-sign a player after he declines their qualifying offer, of course, and it sounds like that path is possible in this case.

Jeffers will decline the QO and the Twins are interested in reaching a multi-year deal to bring him back, reports the Minnesota Star-Tribune. Jeffers hit .256/.353/.461 with 14 home runs for Minnesota in 2026, a standout line for a catcher, though he missed several months with a broken hamate. The Twins do have several catchers in their farm system, including Vahn Lackey, the No. 3 pick in last year's draft, and Eduardo Tait, who headlined the trade return for Jhoan Duran.

Much has been said and will continue to be said about the 2027 free agent class and how it looks relatively weak, especially on the position-player side, where the best players are the likes of Jazz Chisholm Jr., Seiya Suzuki, and the aforementioned Arozarena and Jeffers.

As we know, the Rays love to find avenues where they can exploit market inefficiencies. Their latest move might be to hit the trade market with center fielder Jonny DeLuca in anticipation of moving Victor Mesa Jr. to center, according to The Athletic.

DeLuca, 28, got more playing time than ever before in 2026, appearing in 112 games and getting 370 plate appearances. He hit .266/.300/.429 (101 OPS+) with 11 homers, 50 RBI, 17 steals and 1.7 WAR.

Fresh off a playoff berth despite the lowest payroll in all of baseball at a paltry $75ish million, the Guardians are planning to increase payroll. Or so they say.

"We'll go up," club president Chris Antonetti told The Athletic. "We have to."

The Guardians hosted six playoff games and made some money there, not to mention that they have a bunch of players hitting arbitration and surely they want to spend more to remain competitive. There's an added wrinkle here, too, which would be that the ownership side is really pushing hard for a salary cap when the upcoming CBA expires in a few weeks. With a cap comes a floor and we've seen MLB float proposals with salary floors in the $180 million range, or well more than double what the Guardians had last season.

So, yeah, I'd say the Guardians "have to" increase payroll, one way or another.

#2687. Astros slugger Yordan Alvarez named unanimous American League MVP after nearly winning 2026 Triple Crown

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez has won the 2026 American League MVP, the BBWAA announced Thursday night.

The Baseball Writers' Association of America ballot uses two voters from each of the 15 chapters housing AL teams. Each voter submits a ballot with 10 players, ranked 1-10. A first-place vote gets a player 14 points, while second place earns nine, third place eight, etc., until a 10th-place vote earns one point. Ballots are due before the playoffs begin, as this is a regular-season award.

Alvarez, 29, bounced back from an injury-riddled disaster in 2025, during which he only played in 48 games. This time around, he avoided the IL and appeared in 158 games. He hit .316/.432/.601 (190 OPS+) with 34 doubles, a triple, 42 home runs, 106 RBI, 105 runs and 6.8 WAR. He made a late run at the Triple Crown, missing out by one home run and seven RBI. He did lead the majors in all three triple slash categories, though, leading in average by five points, on-base percentage by a whopping 42 points -- he led the majors in walks -- and 31 points in slugging percentage. Add the latter two and his OPS victory was 90 points -- 1.033 to second place's .943 (National League MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong).

The only players in MLB history to lead the majors in all three triple slash categories:

Alvarez becomes just the third Astros player to win MVP after Jeff Bagwell in 1994 and Jose Altuve in 2017.

Rays third baseman Junior Caminero finished in second. At age 22, he played all 162 games, leading the Rays to the best AL record. He hit .276/.360/.524 (144 OPS+) with 42 home runs, 101 RBI and 100 runs, posting a 5.7 WAR. He's already made history, too, as the Rays had previously never had a player finish in the top five of MVP voting.

Royals shortstop Bobby Witt Jr. came in third. This is now his fourth straight season in the top seven and third straight season in the top four. He finished second in 2024. This season, he hit .281/.359/.441 (125 OPS+) with 33 doubles, 18 homers, 54 RBI, 94 runs, 45 steals and 6.7 WAR.

#2686. Cathedral Prep wins girls soccer state title in overtime

PITTSBURGH – As the bus pulled out of Mechanicsburg in 2024, the Cathedral Prep girls soccer team had one goal in mind.

The hard work and dedication of two years paid off on Saturday, Nov. 21, as the Ramblers beat defending state champion Achbishop Wood 1-0 in overtime in the PIAA Class 2A girls soccer championship at FNB Field.

"This team was here two years ago and it was a tough loss," said Prep standout Anna Johnson. "We had this as our goal before the season and I'm so proud of us all."

Cathedral Prep finishes the season 23-1-1 with its second state title in program history. The other title came in 2015 as Villa Maria.

The Ramblers lost a heartbreaker to Northwestern Lehigh in double overtime in 2024. It didn't sit well with the underclassmen and incoming freshmen.

Prep started working toward getting back to the state final. The Ramblers lost to Burrell in 2025 but stormed back this fall.

After 80 minutes of scoreless soccer, Prep was applying big-time pressure on the Vikings in overtime. Sophomore Lauren McCormick got loose heading down the field and played give-and-go with Jordyn DiRaimo to find open space on the Archbishop Wood side of the field.

McCormick saw she had some forwards to the right so she played a long cross past the net. As Johnson went to take control, her defender collided with the keeper, giving Johnson a wide-open net.

"Lauren had an amazing cross and I knew I had to pressure the goalie," Johnson said. "The ball popped out and I just had to put it in the back of the net."

Johnson's goal sent the Prep side into a frenzy.

"I was driving down the side playing it wide and I knew I had to get it to Anna," McCormick said. "When it went in I just wanted to give her a big hug."

The game winning-goal complemented a shutout effort by Louisville recruit Jordan Senz in goal.

"I just wanted to help my team win," Senz said. "We were a little nervous going in but we had each other's backs."

"Jordan was incredible," said Prep coach Peter Wagner. "She made huge saves to keep us in it. She's an amazing keeper and an amazing kid."

#2683. Washington State blown out by Texas State, 42-14

In their final road game of the season, the Washington State Cougars were dominated by the Texas State Bobcats, 42-14.

WSU (2-9, 1-6 in Pac-12) got in front early with the games' first points on a Daniel Blood touchdown reception, then proceeded to allow 42 unanswered to TSU (7-4, 5-2).

The Cougars got out to a promising start, forcing a three-and-out and converting the first offensive drive into points. They did it in chunks too, starting with a 12-yard run and 10-yard reception from Kirby Vorhees. A roughing the passer on TSU to set WSU up on the TSU-23 yard line, which led to WSU's lone offensive touchdown on the day. Owen Eshelman found Blood on the short curl route, and Blood did the rest. Dodging and dragging Bobcats into the end zone for a 7-0 WSU lead.

It ended up being one of the very few WSU highlights of the night.

The Bobcats immediately answered, scoring on a eight-play, 75-yard drive to tie the game up. WSU's offense went backwards in their response, committing a holding penalty and taking a sack, forcing a quick three-and-out. On the ensuing punt, TSU's Jordan Martin was able to get around the edge and block the punt, giving the Bobcats the ball at WSU's five-yard line. The Cougar defense was able to hold strong on the first two plays but relented on the third on Davian Jackson's third rushing attempt to put the Bobcats up 14-7 early. Despite a promising return by Tank Hawkins Jr., the Cougar drive ended up stalling out. They had a 4th and 3 at the Texas State 37-yard line, but a false start forced their hand into punting from the Bobcat 42.

The Bobcats grinded their way down the field on their fourth drive, finishing it off with a 44-yard QB keeper by Brad Jackson to make the score 21-7.

WSU tried to get back into the game with a long drive that ended up stalling at the Texas State 13-yard line. Jack Stevens trotted out for a field goal attempt from 31 yards out, but the Bobcat special teams came up big again, getting a hand on the field-goal attempt to block it. The Cougar defense would come up big on the ensuing Bobcat drive with a stop on 4th and 5 from the WSU 33-yard line. With 1:12 to go, the Cougar offense more or less decided to run the clock out and get to halftime down 21-7.

The Cougars opened the half with another promising drive that yet again failed around the Bobcat 30-yard line. A 4th and 5 from the TSU 31-yard line ended in an incompletion from Eshelman to Jack Pedersen that officially ended the drive. Following a pair of punts, the Bobcats put together a nine-play, 79-yard drive to put the Bobcats up 28-7.

Another WSU punt gave TSU the ball right back, and another touchdown drive from the Bobcats to put them up 35-7 more or less ended things. WSU did end up getting one more touchdown on the defensive end with a scoop and score to make things look a little closer.

The Cougars may get another shot at Texas State next week depending on the results of the San Diego State vs. Boise State game, as the Pac-12 may flex the Bobcats to Pullman for the final regular season game.

#2682. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Celtics win Jaylen Brown trade (for now), Trae Young looks done

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Every now and then, the NBA gives us a week that is essentially built around a single game. A total of 51 games were played in the last week, but come on, the one you remember was Jaylen Brown's long-awaited reunion with Jayson Tatum. The Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers squared off in a battle of the Eastern Conference's two top seeds on Tuesday, and even if the game fell short of our basketball expectations, it provided more than enough beef to sate us. Brown snubbed Tatum before the game. Paul George gave a fan the middle finger. Appropriate animosity has returned to this eternal rivalry.

So... how did we handle that from a winners and losers perspective? Well, Boston is an obvious winner, but Brown escaped loser status. It's winners and losers of the week. Philly won its two other games this week, and Brown led all scorers in Sunday's win with 31 points. He certainly lost on Tuesday. He may yet wind up losing the trade. But we're not docking him a whole week for a single poor performance. So if Brown escaped the loser's section, who made it? And who joins Boston in the winner's circle? Let's look back at the week that was.

Boston's big win over Philadelphia underlined something that's been evident all season: Paul George, at least thus far, has been better as a Celtic than Jaylen Brown has been as a 76er. There are obviously circumstantial reasons for that. George is at his best as a force-multiplier, and he's on a team on which he doesn't need to play an enormous role. Brown is at his best as a floor-raiser, but he's on a team full of floor-raisers. That doesn't mean Philadelphia regrets the trade -- it got them LeBron James! -- but it does suggest that, after months of criticism, the Celtics at least got what they were looking for out of the deal.

Everything the Celtics were good at a year ago, they're still good at. They were one of the NBA's best shooting teams last season, and George both makes more 3s than Brown and takes far more of them. They were great at protecting the basket last season and George's activity as a helper has been a net benefit to their rim-protection.

Yet George's presence has also been the catalyst for improvement in a few other key areas. Boston never generated turnovers defensively last season and they do this year, in part because George is averaging the sixth-most steals and third-most deflections in the NBA. They're getting to the line at a roughly league-average rate, in part because the ball doesn't stick to George as it so often did Brown. It's easier to get defenses in rotation with the ball moving and 3-pointers flying. Tatum has benefited enormously in this respect with a career-best 46% free-throw rate.

Again, the 76ers are perfectly happy with their end of the deal. They traded old for young. They got James on the minimum. They're 11-3. But Boston emerged with the player who has made a bigger difference thus far this season, and it got two first-round draft assets in the process. That doesn't mean the Celtics necessarily win the trade in the long run, but it does suggest, unsurprisingly, that Brad Stevens understood his own team and what it needed better than the rest of us.

Well, they haven't lost in three weeks... so this feels overdue. Let's talk about the much ballyhooed three-guard lineup for a moment. The Spurs couldn't keep bringing Dylan Harper off the bench this season. He's simply too good and too important to their future to risk alienating. They couldn't bench De'Aaron Fox immediately either. Former All-Stars tend to take such decisions as a sign of disrespect, and such a move could have splintered the locker room.

So the Spurs made the somewhat awkward decision to start the three of them together. The season's second game, a loss to the Houston Rockets, showcased exactly why so many feared the fit of the three of them together. Three iffy guard-sized shooters minimized spacing for the sake of redundant ball-handling, and the Harper-Fox-Stephon Castle trio got outscored by 12 points in a four-point defeat. Well, the three guards haven't lost their minutes together in a single game since then. They're +112 in 115 minutes after that point.

Now, there are notable caveats here. Every three-man combination of Spurs that has played at least 100 minutes since then is firmly positive, and the three guards have literally not played a single minute together this season that did not come alongside Victor Wembanyama. It's entirely possible that Wembanyama is so game-breaking that any lineup he's a part of is an almost automatic winner. But that would work in favor of the three guards here. Maybe San Antonio is so much more talented than the field that it can afford to play suboptimal lineups for the sake of maintaining harmony in the locker room.

That may prove more challenging late in a playoff series, but it's easier to convince players to change their roles for, say, Game 5 of the Western Conference Finals than it is in November or December. The Spurs might have to think harder about this in a field that included a healthy Oklahoma City, but with the Thunder compromised, San Antonio is such a large favorite to win the Western Conference that it can afford to try to just out-talent everyone else. So far, it's clearly working.

We are in all-out panic mode over the state of Cleveland's starting lineup. James Harden can't get to the rim anymore. Donovan Mitchell just signed a supermax extension that already feels iffy. Peyton Watson's shooting has fallen off a cliff and he's struggling as a primary point-of-attack defender. The Evan Mobley-Jarrett Allen partnership is getting crushed in its joint minutes. The starters have played 99 minutes together and lost those minutes by 24 points. No five-man unit that has played that many minutes has been outscored by more. Malaise doesn't do this core justice. Clearly, something here has to change.

Fortunately, there appear to be some internal solutions here. After FAA issues forced the Cavaliers to spend Friday night in Miami, Mitchell called for Saturday's game against the Dallas Mavericks to be postponed. The Cavaliers didn't arrive in Dallas until around noon on Saturday. The starters sat out. Cleveland won the game by 10 against a healthy, playoff-caliber opponent. Tyrese Proctor, Meleek Thomas, Mario Hezonja and Jaylon Tyson all scored between 18 and 24 points.

This wasn't a one-off. Thomas is outscoring Harden and Mobley on a per-minute basis. Proctor is sporting a better-than-6-to-1 assist-to-turnover ratio on the season, and Synergy Sports rates him in the 100th percentile on spot-up efficiency and the 96th in pick-and-rolls, including passes, in terms of points per possession. Tyson breathes life into a transition offense that is otherwise a sore spot. Most of this team's energy comes from the bench.

What exactly the solution here is, we can't say. It will involve a trade. Perhaps a few. But there's something here, and the early indications are that things are going to get better for the team as a whole when it eventually starts leaning on these players a bit more.

Dejounte Murray requested a trade this week. That's not a rumor. The Pelicans publicly acknowledged it and Murray retweeted the news from ESPN. Meanwhile, after Monday's loss to the Golden State Warriors, Jordan Poole was asked if he would ever come back to the team with which he started his career. He answered "yes." Players tend to not be that definitive in those statements, nor do they tend to acknowledge that their former team "just feels like home." It certainly seems as though there's somewhere he'd rather be than New Orleans.

To borrow a phrase from social media user Nathan Calvin, "if you find two ants in your kitchen, the best estimate of the total number of ants in your kitchen is not two." Essentially... if two players seem this eager to flee, more probably do as well. Sam Amick suggested in a radio interview over the summer that Trey Murphy would like to play elsewhere. There has been plenty of speculation about other Pelicans as well. A 4-10 start following 26- and 21-win seasons tends to do that.

We're more than a year into Joe Dumars' reign as head of basketball operations and there's no discernible plan here. Virtually every key player from last year's roster was retained and the team has largely been healthier than it was a year ago, but they're on pace for a worse record under new head coach Jamahl Mosley. The sad thing is that the Pelicans have a fair number of valuable players. They've just assembled those players so carelessly that they've become far less than the sum of their parts. This team is incoherent, and even the players seem to know it.

Trae Young was held scoreless in 26 minutes on Sunday. It was the first time he's been held scoreless in his entire NBA career, but it may be the final straw of a trend that has been bubbling for some time: Trae Young is simply no longer a star-level scorer. He currently has his lowest shooting percentage from both 2-point and 3-point range in a single season. He lacks the burst to get to the rim or beat mismatches consistently anymore, and he's never developed comfort as a catch-and-shooter. Aside from free throws, it's basically all jumpers off the dribble and floaters, neither of which he's making at the rate he needs to in order to justify his defensive shortcomings. He scored 37 points against Detroit last Monday, but needed 17 free throws to get there on less than 35% shooting from the floor. He needs whistles right now.

This is a version of Young who probably shouldn't monopolize an offense, yet he's never shown that he's capable of playing differently. The Wizards are spending 26 possessions a game on shots Young generates either for himself or a teammate out of pick-and-roll, more than any other player in the league, per Synergy Sports. As of Sunday, he and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were tied for the league lead among starters in average seconds possessing the ball per touch, per NBA.com tracking data. The younger players who represent the future of this organization are spending a whole lot of time watching someone else dribble. Nobody is really spacing the floor for anyone else since there's so little shooting on this roster. The Wizards have played close to neutral when Young rests, but are getting outscored by more than 10 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor. That difference is almost entirely offensive, yet Young remains the same defensive liability he's always been.

This is where the four-year max contract Washington bewilderingly gave Young becomes so destructive. The basic notion of acquiring a high-end point guard to serve as an offensive organizer for these young wings made sense on paper, but they committed to him essentially sight unseen. He played five mostly meaningless games in a tanking season and they paid him max money without really knowing how he'd fit with the team they were building. If he'd walked for nothing in free agency, well, it's not as though they spent picks to get him. Now they're stuck paying star-level money for a non-star-level player who probably can't meaningfully scale down his involvement in the offense because he just doesn't provide much value when any other player on either team has the basketball.

There are a lot of things going wrong in Washington right now, but Young is inevitably going to be the face of those struggles because he's the player the Wizards just bewilderingly gave a four-year max contract to in order to re-sign. Jaylen Brown had the loudest individual loss of the week, but he at least won all of his other games and has largely been what his team has asked him to be. Young went winless this week, had a scoreless game, and maintained his mostly disappointing season-long performance.

If you would have heard "the Warriors have a -2.4 net rating a month into the 2026-27 season," you probably would have shrugged and said, "sure, sounds about right." The Warriors were widely pegged as a low-end Play-In, high-end lottery team before the season, and a -2.4 net rating projects out to a win total in the 30s. Except that isn't Golden State's net rating. It's Golden State's net rating in the minutes Stephen Curry has missed this season.

That's how far above expectations Golden State was playing during its eight-game winning streak. The Curry-off version of the team was around average; the Curry-on version of the team was a juggernaut. The latter feels a bit unsustainable, but we won't know again for around a month. The former is what's about to be tested now that Curry has an oblique abdominal tear. The Spurs hardly represent a fair test for a team in this situation, but San Antonio predictably waxed Golden State by 38 in the first game of Curry's absence.

Nobody's asking for another eight-game winning streak. Those wins are banked, and Golden State's season begins in earnest when Jimmy Butler returns in January or February. For now, the Warriors just need to stay afloat. Find wins where the schedule offers them, and fortunately, the Pelicans, Kings, Clippers and Jazz are on the docket in the next three weeks or so. But losing Curry is a reminder of how fragile that streak really was. Maybe, now that Yaxel Lendeborg is emerging as a possible star, the Warriors are capable of genuine postseason success this season. But the health of any 38-year-old not named LeBron James is going to be precarious. Things could be a lot worse, but Curry's injury drags one of the feel-good stories of the early season back down to Earth.

#2681. Weather halts John Carroll-Pahokee region semifinal, tied 14-14 at halftime

FORT PIERCE —The John Carroll Catholic football team was forced to wait nearly a month to line up against another opponent.

With Mother Nature continuing to wreak havoc across Florida, the Rams will have to wait even longer to complete a game.

The conclusion of Saturday's Region 4-1A semifinal matchup between John Carroll and Pahokee was postponed because of unplayable field conditions. The two teams completed one half and headed to the locker rooms tied 14-14 before a weather delay of more than three hours halted the action at McGuire Stadium.

A rescheduled date has not been determined.

When the weather cleared, the teams returned to a field flooded along the sidelines. That's when the game's head official called Rams coach Mickey Groody and Blue Devils coach Carlos Lammons to midfield and informed them the game would not resume.

"He deemed the field unsafe, mainly for his officials, in their workspace in the corner of the end zone," Groody said.

The first of two lightning delays began at 7:22 p.m. Saturday, as fans were asked to exit the stadium. After an hour and 15 minutes, the teams returned to the field and were warming up before the horn sounded for another lightning delay at 8:47 p.m. A torrential downpour soon followed.

The teams again left the locker rooms and returned to the field at 10:18 p.m., but the decision to postpone the game was made as players finished their warmups.

John Carroll last completed a game on Oct. 23, a 28-14 loss at Benjamin.

The Rams (7-3) were scheduled to close the regular season at home against Spruce Creek the following week, but that game was canceled because of unplayable field conditions. Following a postseason bye week, the Rams advanced with a forfeited victory against Somerset Prep in the regional quarterfinals.

"Our kids have done a really good job of dealing with the last few weeks and all the adversity we've had. So to us, it's gonna be business as usual," Groody said. "The makeup, whenever that happens, we'll be ready."

John Carroll struck first when Devon Lewis returned a 20-yard interception return touchdown with 3 minutes, 4 seconds left in the first quarter. The senior defensive back was in the right place at the right time, snagging a bobbled pass off the hands of Blue Devils receiver Samuel Harrigan.

Pahokee answered after getting a short field on the ensuing possession, as a penalty on an onside kick attempt put the ball at the John Carroll 40-yard line. The visitors reached the end zone on the first play of the second quarter thanks to an 8-yard touchdown run by Decorrian Jones.

After a Craig Lawrence interception, the Blue Devils scored again on a short field. They traveled 23 yards in five plays, capped by a 3-yard touchdown run from Mari Singleton.

The Rams tied the game with a seven-play, 79-yard drive just before halftime.

Three big gains on quarterback keepers by junior Carter Cullen and an 18-yard rush from senior tailback Jaydien Pittman quickly put the Rams at the Pahokee 28. Cullen connected with Pittman on a 26-yard reception before Pittman punched in a 1-yard touchdown run.

John Carroll finished with 148 yards of total offense.

The regional semifinal is a rematch of a District 10-1A game played Sept. 25. John Carroll earned a 23-20 victory that night after Pahokee missed a potential game-tying field goal late in the fourth quarter. The Rams won the district title at the end of the regular season, capturing a three-team tiebreaker over the Blue Devils and Benjamin.

Patrick Bernadeau is a sports reporter for Treasure Coast Newspapers. He can be reached at 772-985-9692, on X at @PatBernadeau or via email at pbernadeau@gannett.com.

#2680. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2679. Now with an MVP, Pete Crow-Armstrong is on the path for an all-time great career. Where could he stack up?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The MVP winners were revealed Thursday evening and, unsurprisingly, the runaway unanimous winner in the National League was Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Cubs.

Crow-Armstrong had an all-time great regular season, which is what the annual Baseball Writers' Association of America award honors. He hit .280/.372/.570 with stellar defense, led the league in home runs (tied with Kyle Schwarber) and massively upgraded his on-base skills. Now, just a few months shy of his 25th birthday, he has an MVP to his name.

So what's next? To answer that, we'll look backwards.

Since integration, only eight center fielders have posted at least 8.0 WAR in a season age-25 or younger: Willie Mays, Mickey Mantle, Willie Davis, César Cedeño, Ken Griffey Jr., Andruw Jones, Mike Trout and PCA. The only ones to top PCA's 9.8 were Mays, Mantle and Trout. If we went back to pre-integration, Tris Speaker and Ty Cobb were the only others who bested PCA here.

Willie Davis was an inconsistent hitter through his age-23 season but had flashed a nice power-speed combo. Sound familiar? That gaudy 8.4 WAR total in 1964, though, was driven largely by monster defensive metrics. Davis hit .294/.316/.413 (110 OPS+) with 23 doubles, seven triples, 12 home runs, 77 RBI, 91 runs and 42 steals. There's little doubt that PCA's 2026 season dwarfed this one overall, and Davis was far behind Mays (11.0) for the league lead in WAR.

For the rest of his career, Davis averaged 3.1 WAR per season, and though he had good years, he never reached 6.0 WAR again. The WAR figure was, again, mostly driven by defense. He had several good offensive seasons, but his only 20-homer season came in 1962 when he was 22, two years prior to his career year.

Davis' career probably looks a lot like PCA's apparent upside before his home run barrage in the first half of 2025. He racked up over 60 career WAR with a decent batting average, excellent defense and excellent baserunning.

With PCA reaching 30-30 last year and 40-40 this year, though, the bar has been raised.

César Cedeño followed up his 8.0 WAR season with a 7.4 season at age 22 and 5.8 at age 23. He was very good through age 29 and, in fact, the most statistically similar player through both ages 27 and 28 was Hall of Famer Carl Yastrzemski. Things fell apart after that. As a quick and easy way to illustrate it, Cedeño amassed 49.4 WAR through his age-29 season and only 3.6 in his final six years.

It's easier to remember that Andruw Jones' career unfolded in similar fashion because we witnessed it not too long ago and then discussed his Hall of Fame candidacy during his nine turns on the ballot before he finally made it in. In Jones' 12 Braves' season, he racked up 368 home runs, 1,117 RBI and 61 WAR while generally being considered the best defensive center fielder in baseball. Once he left, in time for his age-31 season, Jones accrued just 1.7 WAR in his last five seasons.

Through Jones' age-28 season, the most statistically similar players are Bryce Harper and Frank Robinson.

To compare these two to Crow-Armstrong, the argument would be that he'll continue to look like one of the best players in baseball -- even if taking steps backward from being the very best in the 2026 regular season -- before falling apart once he's around 30 years old.

Certainly possible, but given the adjustments he's already not only been willing to make at the plate, but eager to make, I'm just not seeing him all of a sudden hitting a wall. Sure, at some point he'll start losing speed and that'll affect his defensive range and baserunning, but why would the plate skills deteriorate all of a sudden?

Then again, few saw it coming with Jones.

All three of these players were on the path to having an argument as the best player in history before injuries derailed them in their 30s and left them as mere "all-time greats."

Through Mickey Mantle's age-30 season, he had 90.7 WAR. He averaged 121 games per year in his final six seasons, putting up 19.5 WAR. Through  Ken Griffey Jr.'s age-30 season, he had 76.2 WAR. He played 10 more seasons, but only amassed 7.6 more WAR. Through Mike Trout's age-27 season, he had 72.1 WAR (his top statistical similars were Mantle, Robinson and Griffey). We'll skip 2020 for obvious reasons, but since then he's averaged 90 games and 3.0 WAR per season.

Even with the drop-offs, it would be surprising to see Crow-Armstrong reach this level because it's surprising to see any player reach this lofty standard. In career WAR among center fielders, Mantle is fourth, Trout is fifth and Griffey is sixth. They trail only Cobb, Speaker and the guy we're going to discuss next. Joe DiMaggio is seventh.

Despite the lofty standard PCA set for himself in 2026, coming close to Willie Mays' career would be jaw-droppingly shocking, and that is absolutely not intended as a slight.

Mays has an argument as the greatest player in baseball history and he put himself in that discussion by being good at everything and doing it all with great longevity. From his age-23 to -35 seasons, he led the majors in WAR eight times, leading the NL an additional two times. His worst seasons in that timeframe were 7.6 and 7.8 WAR. In that span, he also led the league in runs twice, hits once, triples three times, home runs three times, stolen bases four times, average once, on-base percentage once, slugging percentage five times and OPS five times.

Mays even posted 5.2 WAR at age 39 and 6.3 at age 40. He led the NL with a .425 OBP when he was 40 years old! He hit .345/.411/.667 at age 23.

Mays' 156.2 career WAR ranks third among position players all-time behind two guys you might have heard of: Barry Bonds (162.8) and Babe Ruth (162.3).

I feel pretty strongly Pete Crow-Armstrong isn't headed for a run at this career and that's just fine.

The realistic long-term range for the 2026 National League MVP seems somewhere between Cedeño and Mantle. It's a wide variance of outcomes between those two, obviously, as well it should be when the player we discuss is only 24 years old. For his name to be mentioned among these at all is a testament to the year Crow-Armstrong just put together.
