#2578. The wistful romanticism of ÍA, the club that once ruled Iceland against the odds

A little over 30 miles to the north of Reykjavik resides the small port town of Akranes on Iceland’s west coast. Even for Iceland, this is not a huge place. With its buildings gathered on a thin sliver of a peninsula that extends furtively into the ocean, it is home to a mere 8,000 inhabitants.

Like many coastal settlements in Iceland, Akranes is noted for its thriving fishing industry, and its deep, still harbour is home to a flotilla of trawlers that combs these teeming waters each summer.  But there is another reason that Akranes is a name familiar to many Icelanders, and it has nothing to do with trawlermen.

Those who do not take to the waves in search of fish prefer to take to the football field in search of a more prestigious catch. The town’s resident football team, Íþróttabandalag Akraness, more commonly referred to by their initials ÍA, are one of Iceland’s most successful clubs. It is a remarkable feat given that for much of its 75-year existence, the club has been bound by its rural location and small population.

The roots of this success were planted deep in the earth of the 20th century when in 1951 ÍA became the first club outside of Reykjavik to secure the Úrvalsdeild karla title – literally, the Men’s Select Division. For the first 39 years of the league’s existence, the Reykjavik clubs of Knattspyrnufélag Reykjavíkur (KR), Valur, Vikingur and Knattspyrnufélagið Fram had exerted an unshakeable oligopoly over Iceland’s elite football division.

But throughout the latter half of the century, as the league moved beyond a single-round to a double-round format, the inhabitants of this small fishing town became famed for their excellence on the football pitch. Between 1951 and 1990, no club was as successful in Iceland as ÍA, and much of this domestic dominance was attributed to the labours of Ríkharður Jonsson, who acted as long-time player-manager.

Sadly, he passed away in 2017, but These Football Times was privileged enough to speak with his daughter, Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir, with help from his grandson, Ríkharður Árnason. Sigrún has been attending ÍA matches her entire life and is as fervent a Skagamenn supporter as they come. “You don’t want to sit next to me at a game,” she says drily. “I am the loudest woman in Iceland when it comes to the football!” Meanwhile, her son shares his first name with the legendary figure of his grandfather and is head of social media at the club. Few, if any, can claim a richer heritage with this unique football club.

Their past and their future are incorrigibly entwined with that of Íþróttabandalag Akraness, and it is in their past that this tale begins. In 1990, to be precise, whereupon ÍA had suffered relegation for only the second time in their history. Though they had won the league twice and the Icelandic Cup four times throughout the 1980s, by the turn of the decade the club had somehow contrived to slip through the dreaded trapdoor into the First League.

“You know how football is,” Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir says with a wry smile when asked to explain what went wrong for the then-12-time champions. “Sometimes you have a good game. Sometimes you have a bad game. But the team from ’83 and ’84 were gone, and the next generation we had taking over were young – very young, indeed.”

The ÍA team that suffered the infamy of relegation was heavily reliant on a core of young and painfully inexperienced footballers. Several of the players who featured in every, or almost every, league game included left winger Haraldur Ingólfsson (20-years-old), midfielder/left-back Sigursteinn Gíslason (22) and future superstar striker Arnar Gunnlaugsson, who was the team’s joint top-scorer that season at the mere age of 17.

Admirable though it was to entrust the fortunes of the club in the hands (and feet) of youth, the result for ÍA was painful. Playing football in the second tier for the first time since 1968, this predicament only consolidated the view in Reykjavik that Akranes was simply a town of chancers who had punched far above their weight for far too long and were now reaping what they’d sown in their foolhardy attempts to meddle with the might of the capital.

Realising that the club had been allowed to slowly decay throughout the latter half of the 1980s, the board turned to one of its former stalwarts to invigorate an inexperienced squad in need of firm guidance. ÍA legend and all-time appearance holder, Guðjón Þórðarson, was persuaded to rejoin the club at which he had found fame in his playing days.

One of the last relics of the 1980s golden era, since retiring in 1987 he had ventured into coaching and his innovative training methods, which placed an enormous emphasis on fitness, discipline and recovery, had seen virtual unknowns KA Akureyri crowned champions for the first time in their history by virtue of being fitter, faster and better organised than their contemporaries.

He was a man in high demand, but with KA lacking the finances required to repeat this success in subsequent seasons, the chance of a reunion with ÍA proved too alluring to ignore. Even though it necessitated dropping down a division, he agreed to become head coach and began in earnest restoring ÍA to the Úrvalsdeild karla.

The only previous time ÍA had suffered relegation had resulted in an immediate return to the top flight, whereupon they finished second, before going one better and winning the league the following year in 1970. Accordingly, great things were expected of this dynamic side brimming with youthful vigour, and under the strict stewardship of Þórðarson, they were being moulded into a formidable outfit.

Serendipity deigned to alight upon ÍA who, despite playing football in the unglamorous environment of Iceland’s second division, managed to attract the services of three players patently too talented for their surroundings. First, Þórðarson – who was renowned for travelling extensively on his scholastic enterprises – spotted the hulking figure of Olafur Adolfsson in the amateur leagues of Iceland’s sparse northern marches and brought him to Akranes. At well over six feet tall and broad of shoulder and limb too, Adolfsson struck an uncompromising figure at the heart of the ÍA back line.

Alongside this mountain of a man, Þórðarson installed Luka Kostic, a Yugoslav centre-half who is, even to this day, widely regarded as the finest foreign footballer to have ever played in Iceland, even though he was 33 at the time of his arrival. Bringing with him a wealth of expertise, he was responsible for marshalling those around him.

Boasting an impregnable defence aided by the capture from bitter rivals KR of 20-year-old goalkeeper Kristján Finnbogason, ÍA made predictably short work of returning to the top flight. Across 18 second division games in 1991, the club won 14, scored 55 goals and conceded a paltry 12 in reply. Úrvalsdeild karla football ensured for the 1992 campaign, hope slunk back into Akranes. With the most innovative young manager in the country presiding over a hungry, well-drilled squad of saplings primed to flourish come spring, there was a feeling ÍA could cause an upset.

However, since Skagamenn’s last championship victory in 1984, Fram and Valur had asserted their domestic dominance. The two traditionally powerful Reykjavik clubs had won five of the previous seven titles, and on three occasions occupied first and second places in the league. Even with ÍA’s return, the title was widely expected to remain in the capital, at least for another year. From the outside, the yellow-clad upstarts from Akranes were still too inexperienced to mount a serious title challenge so soon after the turmoil of relegation and were written off by pundits, supporters and near enough anyone with even a passing interest in Icelandic football.

However, before the season began in 1992, ÍA were to benefit from one more fortuitous occurrence, one which would have a major bearing on their fortunes for years to come, as Þórðarson convinced former player Sigurður Jónsson to make the long trip back to his hometown.

Only 25-years-old at the time, the prodigious midfielder had been forced to retire prematurely after suffering a back injury while playing for Arsenal in England’s old First Division but was coaxed into playing once more for the club at which he made his debut aged just 15. A veritable legend of the sport in Iceland, he was the erstwhile youngest debutant in a European game before being supplanted by a certain Martin Ødegaard some years later.

Much to the chagrin of the Reykjavik clubs – and in particular their fierce rivals KR – ÍA furnished their return to the Úrvalsdeild karla with their 13th championship and their first in nearly a decade.

It was a momentous achievement, which Ríkharðsdóttir ascribes in part, at least, to patience. “Many of the boys who were with us when we fell down to the First League stayed with us and these young lads just got stronger and better [under Þórðarson].”

Inclined to set-up in a four-four-two system that harnessed a squad accustomed to gruelling training regimens, the ÍA players ran harder and for longer, were physically stronger and, as is crucial to any team with ambitions of winning a league, possessed an indomitable mental resilience in pursuit of their goals. That they could play, too, was an added benefit.

Although it is not unheard of for clubs to win the title immediately after promotion, especially in the Nordic countries where the traditionally smaller leagues are somewhat renowned for producing surprise victors, seldom have many teams managed to repeat the feat. Indeed, miraculously, ÍA became the first club in the history of football to not only win the league following promotion but win it for five consecutive seasons.

Just how could a team hailing from a town of barely 8,000 people, and who had been relegated just a year earlier, undertake a championship run the likes of which had never been witnessed in Iceland in over a century of organised sport? Not just Iceland, either, but anywhere in the entire world. At the time, no team had won five championships in a row directly after being promoted. It was an idea born from fiction; a feat literally unbelievable in its design.

Ríkharðsdóttir, however, believes she has the answer. “It was the same team. All the five years. And the manager, too. In 1992, 1993, and 1996 we had the same manager [Guðjón Þórðarson].”

This continuity undoubtedly benefited ÍA, but there was another factor at play, one which, in the long roster of champions not just in Iceland but across the continent of Europe, is unquestionably unique. Though many claim to be ‘close-knit family clubs’ nowhere is it more pertinent than in Akranes, where, it is said, “everyone is related somewhere”.

Of ÍA’s squad, eight were sons of former players, seven were brothers, six were cousins, three were nephews and, in a testament to the longevity of this dynasty, one was even a grandson. Ríkharðsdóttir herself, being the daughter of the club’s most famous player, claims a deep affinity within this 1990s vintage side. “In that team at the beginning of the 1990s, I had four uncles. In fact, lots of good local players are in the same families here,” she explains.

It is an entirely unique footballing dynasty; a positive myriad of interrelated riches. But clearly, as the old adage goes, there is something in the water in Akranes, for such a small town to repeatedly produce an unbroken line of talent that coaching alone cannot surely engender. Genetics play their part, and Ríkharðsdóttir explains with an air of pride the stats behind her town’s unmatched footballing pedigree. “We have had 38 players [as of 2021] that have played professionally abroad. That is 0.5 percent of the town’s current population who are or were professional footballers playing around the world.”

Given the small size of town, it is scarcely believable that this tiny strip of land on Iceland’s west coast has been so prolific in producing such talented footballers. Fortunately for ÍA in the 1990s, they profited from the particularly abundant vintage of 1973, which produced the likes of Arnar Gunnlaugsson, Þórður Guðjónsson and Lárus Orri Sigurðsson, all of whom were raised and nurtured in Akranes. Though they went on to enjoy careers in England’s Premier League, it was their exploits between 1992 and 1996 that earned them acclaim in their town of provenance.

Over the course of five years, ÍA stormed to five consecutive league titles. After the first was secured on their return to the Úrvalsdeild karla by a three-point margin, a rivalry that had been put on pause during their relegation reignited. Enmity had been simmering between ÍA and KR in the years prior to 1992, and with the latter enduring a protracted silverware drought, the notion of ÍA returning to the pinnacle of Icelandic football rekindled this latent wrath.

The 1993 season, therefore, was billed as a clash between two eternal enemies, but, once again, pundits and observers alike dismissed ÍA’s chances of repeating their 1992 success. At the time in the early-90s, KR were the only club capable of paying their players anything close to what would now be regarded as a professional salary, and as such could attract the finest players to West Reykjavik. Their riches could not stop ÍA romping to a second title in two years, however.

If anything, ÍA were, to the surprise of many, merely waxing in strength. In 1992, they had amassed 40 points from 12 wins and four draws, but in 1993 they finished top of the pile with an incredulous 49 points – a full nine points clear of nearest challengers FH. Indeed, only Fram took any points whatsoever off Skagamenn that year. The rest of the league stumbled in their efforts to keep up with the early pace set by Þórðarson’s insatiable side. On no fewer than seven occasions, ÍA scored four or more goals in a single game, including an opening day 5-0 demolition of eventual runners-up FH.

Þórður Guðjónsson, of the famed 1973 vintage, finished as both club and league top scorer with 19 goals, while 22-year-old winger Haraldur Ingólfsson was not far behind with 14. Moreover, that ÍA could outscore virtually anyone was daunting enough, but their resolute backline was breached only 12 times all season – and seven of those came during the two fixtures with Fram.

It was inevitable, then, that ÍA would march to a third title in a row in 1994, but not without KR attempting everything in their power to ensure otherwise. After they had finished in a lowly fifth in 1993, having been unceremoniously thumped by ÍA to the tune of five goals over two fixtures, the Reykjavik giants sought to undercut their rivals the only way they knew how: money. They lured manager Guðjón Þórðarson to the KR-völlur and secured the return of goalkeeper Kristján Finnbogason. Little did it matter, though, for Þórðarson had bred a monster even he himself could not slay, no matter the riches with which he tempered his sword.

KR finished fifth again, while ÍA clinched a hat-trick of championships. Not that the season was without its struggles. In the absence of Þórðarson, the board had appointed Hörður Helgason, and though he won the title, he was more alike to a custodian than manager. Compared to 1992, when Skagamenn had marched to 16 wins, they faltered to three 0-0 draws and three losses in a season which saw their goal tally plummet from 55 to 35. Mistrusted by the players, who allegedly did not approve of his outdated coaching methods, he was dismissed at the end of the year and replaced with Logi Ólafsson.

Þórðarson, meanwhile, attempted to navigate KR back to the summit of the Úrvalsdeild karla in 1994 and perhaps would have done so had Olafsson not reinvigorated ÍA with his arrival. Yet again, the club came perilously close to that elusive unbeaten campaign, as they registered just a single loss – ironically, to Þórðarson’s KR side, who would eventually finish a very distant second to their bitter rivals. For the fourth season in a row, an ÍA player finished as the league’s top scorer; this time, it was another member of the 1973 vintage, Arnar Gunnlaugsson, who completed the campaign with 15 goals to his name.

In 1996, Þórðarson, whose affair with KR had come to an unsavoury end, returned to the club, looking to secure a fifth consecutive title and his third with ÍA. Astonishingly, KR were installed as the strong favourites for the title, and for once, the bookies were almost right.

For the first time in five years, Iceland witnessed an enthralling title race between two heated enemies, where over the course of 17 games, the two clubs exchanged places at the top of the table before a final-day show down at the Akranesvöllur. KR had emerged victorious in the return fixture, a 1-0 win courtesy of a 68th-minute Ríkharður Daðason goal, but the final day clash is a day Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir recalls fondly, and for more than one reason. “In 1996, in the last game we played against KR, and KR needed just a draw to win the title. But we had to win. And, oh my god, we did. Four goals against one.”

ÍA, who had been trailing KR for much of the campaign, demonstrated the enormous mental resolve for which they had become renowned, and overhauled the leaders on the final day of the season. Knowing that a draw was all KR required, they tore into their opponents, going 2-0 up by the hour-mark before Ríkharður Daðason pulled one back to set up a nervy final twenty minutes. It is a name familiar to many in Akranes, especially Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir.

“The scorer for the KR goal was [her son] Rikki’s uncle and namesake! For that one goal he scored that game, he won the golden boot.”

Unfortunately for Sigrún Ríkharðsdóttir, Ríkharður Árnason and the inhabitants of Akranes, the 1996 league and cup double marked the end of a record-breaking cycle. By 1997, the yellow-and-black stranglehold on the Úrvalsdeild karla had slackened, but the relinquishing of their throne was at least a slow and reluctant process, for ÍA still managed to finish second in 1997, then third in 1998 and even reigned as champions again, albeit briefly, in 2001.

What precipitated the downfall of their monopoly was a convergence of many factors, Ríkharðsdóttir believes. “Our key players have gone away, both to play abroad and for other teams in Iceland. For me, it’s extremely difficult to watch my boys play for other teams in Iceland.”

This assertion harks back to the notion that football in Akranes remains very much a familial affair. Those who come through the ranks at ÍA are Skagamenn until the end of their days, even if their travels are increasingly taking them farther and farther from home.

“It is also a question of money,” Ríkharðsdóttir continues. “The main thing today is that because we are not in European competition, we do not have enough money. Our players prefer to go abroad. One of our players is in CSKA Moscow [Arnór Sigurðsson] and one of our boys plays for Norrköping [Oliver Stefánsson].”

Similarly, prodigious winger Ísak Bergmann Jóhannesson, who has drawn the attention of a host of clubs across the continent, plies his trade with FC København, while Stefán Teitur Þórðarson went to Silkeborg in Denmark and Bjarki Steinn Bjarkason is enjoying Serie A football with Venezia.

Unfortunately for ÍA, when the club was in its pomp in the early to mid-90s, European qualification was nowhere near as lucrative as it is today. They made fleeting appearances in the UEFA Champions League preliminary round in 1993 and the UEFA Cup first round between 1994 and 1997, but without the enormous financial rewards gleaned by the continental voyages of today’s top teams in Iceland.

As such, it has been a long 20 years since the club’s last title in 2001. An Icelandic Cup victory in 2003 and a runners-up medal in 2021 have provided scant solace for the proud people of Akranes who grow ever more restless with each barren season. This two-decade stretch marks the longest period in their history they have gone without winning the league, and in that time they have been relegated twice, albeit returning to the top flight at the first time of asking on both occasions.

There have been no more five-in-a-row heroics, though, as an increasingly globalised world, which has seen Icelandic football broadcast to the rest of Europe for the first time in the league’s history, has led on one hand to a diaspora of Akranes’ young footballers and on the other to an influx of foreign talent to the traditionally powerful Reykjavik clubs.

Silverware will return, the people of Akranes believe; after all, their town is the fastest growing settlement in all of Iceland, and therein lies a sliver of hope. Amidst the squabbling rich boys of Reykjavik, there still may be a place for the wistful romanticism of ÍA. Perhaps, in years to come, another legacy in yellow-and-black will emerge from this westerly stronghold of dynastic riches – born of fresh blood within which is carried the blueprint of that unrivalled 1990s vintage.

With thanks to Sígrun Ríkharðsdóttir, Ríkharður Árnason, Bjarki Ármannsson and Mike Morgan.

#2577. Luis Castillo trade grades: White Sox give up steady back-end starter to offload salary; Rockies get creative

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Two days after adding Dustin May to their rotation, the Chicago White Sox have subtracted Luis Castillo and Davis Martin. The White Sox are sending Castillo and Martin to the Colorado Rockies for lefty Sean Sullivan and minor-league catcher Douglas Veliz, the teams announced late Thursday. The Rockies will take on Castillo's entire contract.

Castillo, 33, joined the White Sox in a deadline trade with the Seattle Mariners. He struggled badly after the deal, allowing 30 runs in 31 innings, and he finished the season on the injured list with a shoulder issue. Castillo has one year remaining on his contract at $22.75 million, though a $25 million option for 2028 will vest if he throws 150 innings in 2027.

The 29-year-old Martin threw 146 innings with a 3.95 ERA in 2026, but it was a 3.41 ERA in the first half and a 5.12 ERA in the second half. The White Sox kept him at arm's length in the postseason despite running bullpen games almost nightly. Martin allowed two runs in one inning in his only postseason appearance.

Neither Sullivan nor Veliz are significant prospects. For all intents and purposes, the White Sox are attaching Martin to Castillo as a sweetener to get the Rockies to take Castillo's salary. The Rockies are essentially buying Martin, who is under team control through 2030, by taking on the rest of Castillo's contract.

Here now are our trade grades for this two-for-two swap.

Fair or not, I'm going to lump the two Castillo trades together. Chicago stepped out to acquire Castillo at the deadline and absorbed the $30 million or so remaining on his contract to do it. Seranthony Domínguez, who had about $15 million left on his deal, went the other way in the trade, so the White Sox took on about $15 million total, and also gave up a pretty good prospect in Boston Smith.

Four and a half months later, the White Sox had to give up a steady back-end starter in Martin to clear Castillo's money. They ended up saving about $7 million in 2027 in this series of moves, but it cost them Martin and Smith (and Domínguez), and they had to endure 31 awful innings from Castillo. Unless Sullivan or Veliz hit big, the White Sox took a series of Ls here.

Credit to president of baseball operations Chris Getz for acknowledging a mistake with Castillo and acting quickly to unload him. It was costly, though. Martin isn't a star, but cheap back-end starters are very valuable. We'll see what Getz & Co. do with the savings. Presumably they'll invest in more pitching. Having to give up Martin to dump Castillo so soon is a stinker, though. Ouch.

The Rockies need all types of pitching (righty, lefty, starter, reliever, whatever) and it's not often they can convince quality (or even competent) free agents to come to Coors Field. They have to develop their own pitchers or trade for pitching, and in this instance, they took on Castillo's hefty salary to get Martin and his four years of control. Creative, if nothing else.

There is downside potential too. Martin has run below league-average strikeout rates and middling ground ball rates throughout his career. Pitchers who allow a lot of balls in play -- a lot of balls in play in the air -- are a poor match for Coors Field. It's good the Rockies spent and found a way to add controllable pitching. They just might not have picked the best pitcher.

After losing 104 games in 2026, there is no such thing as a bad dart throw for the Rockies. It's unlikely they would have been able to spend the $22.75 million on a free agent (at least not without overpaying), so taking on Castillo to get Martin is the next best thing. I like the thinking, even if I don't love Martin's profile in Coors Field.

#2576. Kyrie Irving to the Jazz? Why Utah's reported interest in the star Mavericks guard makes no sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NBA teams are remarkably diligent. They will consider almost any path to improving their rosters, no matter how obscure or unexpected. Still, every now and then, a truly bizarre nugget hits the rumor mill and forces us to consider what exactly a team is thinking.

On Thursday, one such rumor arrived as SNY's Ian Begley reported that the Utah Jazz have given Kyrie Irving "internal consideration as a potential trade candidate." Now, this is common. Teams will do due diligence on a wide variety of players leading up to transaction periods in order to make sure they've covered their bases, and Begley gives no indication that there have even been talks between the Jazz and the Dallas Mavericks. Still, as he notes, "you're not gonna spend a lot of time on a player if you don't have any interest in him, so the idea of Utah spending some time internally on Kyrie Irving was interesting."

So, let's consider this rumor in earnest. The Jazz entered this season with playoff expectations after four straight years in the lottery. They are 3-13 due to a combination of injuries, players adjusting to a new roster and simply poor performance. Utah has shown a willingness to trade for players outside of its perceived timeline before. The Jazz looked at then-33-year-old Jrue Holiday early in their rebuild in 2023, for instance, but backed off when Holiday's camp reportedly made it clear he would not be interested in extending.

Irving, still a star-caliber scorer, has the Mavericks at 8-7 through 15 games. He's averaging over 22 points on roughly his standard efficiency for a Dallas team with pretty limited shooting around him. We can't say at this stage whether or not the Mavericks are willing to trade him. The notion that they might depends on the team's asset deficit (Dallas does not control its own first-round pick again until 2031) and the 15-year age gap between Irving and franchise player Cooper Flagg, but Dallas could easily elect to simply build off this early success.

If they do take the long view and consider trade offers, Irving could absolutely help a team trying to win right now. Plenty of teams potentially looking for individual shot-creation, like the Detroit Pistons, Houston Rockets and Miami Heat, could be planning pursuits of the future Hall of Famer.

The question here is why the Jazz, specifically, would be interested in Irving, because on paper, there is perhaps not a single, high-profile player who makes less sense for this roster than he does. Utah's young core revolves around three perimeter players: Keyonte George, Darryn Peterson and Ace Bailey. The Jazz are so strong on that front that Bailey came off the bench to start the season, and it's unclear how exactly they plan to handle their starting five when Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. return from injuries. If Utah isn't comfortable with Jackson playing center full time, and the Memphis Grizzlies certainly weren't, then one of those five players either needs to get traded or come off the bench.

Adding Irving to this logjam doesn't make sense. Neither does trading one of those players for Irving. George is 23. Bailey is 20. Peterson is 19. Teams that are 10 games below .500 simply don't trade foundational pieces for players a decade or more their senior. They gave up three first-round picks for Jackson largely to improve their defense, and now that Walker Kessler plays for the Los Angeles Lakers, his presence matters more than ever.

Markkanen is the obvious trade candidate of the group, but he's still five years younger than Irving and plays a less saturated position. If Utah viewed Markkanen's max contract as a negative it needed to escape, that would be one thing, but there's just no evidence at this stage that this is the case. They have rebuffed trade interest in Markkanen at every turn. If Dallas were willing to put substantial draft equity on the table to cover the age and positional gaps here, there could perhaps be a conversation, but Dallas isn't in a position to do so.

There's some merit to the idea that Utah might eventually want to shake up its backcourt. There were rumors during the draft process that Peterson's representatives were skeptical of Utah as a landing spot because they also represent George and felt that two score-first guards would clash. Even if the Jazz were prepared to split them up less than 20 games into Peterson's career, Irving himself has typically fared far better when he has been paired with a high-level passer. He won his championship with LeBron James. He's thriving next to Cooper Flagg now. His best trait is, and always has been, his scoring.

And then, of course, there is the history shared between Irving and Utah's top executive. The CEO of the Jazz is Danny Ainge, who once traded for Irving when he ran the Boston Celtics. Before his second season in Boston, Irving publicly shared plans to re-sign with the Celtics as a free agent in 2019. When the time came, he instead joined the Brooklyn Nets, a divisional opponent. This is the NBA. If LeBron James can reunite with Dan Gilbert, any player-executive reunion is theoretically possible. Nonetheless, Ainge and Irving would seemingly be among the unlikeliest pairings in all of basketball. Put all of this together and this is a puzzling rumor to say the least.

Sometimes a rumor says more about a team's big-picture plans than it does a specific target. For a variety of reasons, some of which we've covered, it seems exceedingly unlikely that the Jazz are going to trade for Irving. However, they've invested the time in considering it, as Begley noted. That means something, even if it doesn't mean a trade is coming.

The simplest read on this is that Utah is concerned enough about its short-term prospects that it is considering investing in win-now help despite its 3-13 start. That, in itself, makes sense. The Jazz don't control their own first-round pick this season. They have no incentive to lose, and while making the postseason despite starting the season 10 games under .500 is improbable, it just happened a year ago when the 4-14 Charlotte Hornets recovered quickly enough to reach the Play-In Tournament. The Jazz are 5.5 games out of the No. 10 seed in the Western Conference right now. If they get healthy in time and make the right addition, perhaps they could still make a real run at it.

Skepticism about the George-Peterson fit, for now, should be on the back burner. Though the two fared far better early on when they played separately, both, at least for now, have better net ratings and true shooting percentages in the minutes they've shared than the minutes they haven't. George's usage skyrockets when he plays without Peterson, but that's to be expected with Markkanen and Jackson out.

There may have been concern early in the season, and that might have been when Irving crossed Utah's mind. There may still be concerns down the line when the Jazz have had a longer sample size to evaluate the pairing with the rest of their roster. For now, though, it's simply too early to consider splitting up such a talented tandem, especially right as the team has actually started winning some games.

However, ball-handling behind them is a valid concern. Utah declined its fourth-year option on backup point guard and former first-round pick Isaiah Collier, and the offense has been 6.5 points per 100 possessions worse with him on the floor this season. Adding a veteran backup point guard, if only to ease Peterson's burden during the minutes George rests, would be sensible. Irving is obviously no backup, but as perhaps the most notable point guard theoretically on the market, it makes sense that the Jazz would at least broach the concept internally.

Ainge hasn't earned the nickname "Trader Danny" for nothing. His teams are almost always at the center of the trade market, and as last year's Jackson deal proved, he's as capable of a stunner as he's ever been. Irving would certainly qualify as one. We shouldn't expect it. It wouldn't really make sense based on what we know now. But in the post-Luka Dončić trade NBA, it would be hard to dismiss basically any rumor involving a player of this stature.

#2575. Patriots WR A.J. Brown expected to miss multiple weeks due to hamstring injury, per report

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The injuries for the New England Patriots continue to pile up. Wide receiver A.J. Brown is expected to miss multiple weeks with a hamstring injury, per reports. The news comes the same day as reports that quarterback Drake Maye is expected to miss most, if not all, of the remainder of the regular season with a broken right fibula.

Brown suffered the hamstring injury during their Week 10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Germany. The 29-year-old has dealt with numerous injuries this season, finding himself on the injury report more times than not.

The three-time Pro Bowler suffered an ankle injury in their season opener and was placed on injured reserve, missing four games. After he returned, he then missed two games due to a knee strain.

What started as a slew of hopeful possibilities for the Patriots, with Brown and Maye leading the offense, has dipped quite dramatically. The duo has played together in just four games this season, and in those four games, Brown has 11 receptions for 128 yards and no touchdowns.

The Patriots are currently on a bye, but even with the extra time to rest, Brown is expected to be sidelined for multiple games.

The wide receiver room now consists of Mack Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism and Kyle Williams. Romeo Doubs will be eligible to return from IR when the team returns from its bye week.

The Patriots acquired Brown this offseason from the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for a 2027 fifth-round pick and a 2028 first-round pick.

New England currently sits at 5-5 and will face the Los Angeles Chargers when it returns from the bye in Week 12.

#2574. Talking to Icarus Football, the kit designers adding beauty to the game

“Football shirts give off a lot of signals,” Robby Smukler says. “They can indicate what you’re passionate about, where you’re from, and even your politics in some cases. That’s part of what makes them so special as a piece of clothing—there’s really so much that’s tied into a football shirt.”

It’s easy to agree with that sentiment. Combining place, philosophy, art, design, and, for some, religion and a sense of belonging, football shirts are the acceptable fashion piece that allow anyone to make a splash and stand out from the crowd. Whether worn at a match, at a festival, or for a quick trip to the coffee house, jerseys are the accessible statement piece anyone can pull off (or on) with ease.

You might also say that they’re a great way of telling your nosey Red neighbour that you’re a die-hard Blue in that silent “fuck you” kind of way.

Robby is the founder of Icarus Football, a custom kit design service making tailor-made shirts for everyone, from five-a-side teams to semi-pro outfits. Quintessentially one-of-a-kind, their jerseys offer one-off pieces that faithfully highlight the sui generis of each club.

Robby’s dream of being a creative started many years ago when he became fascinated with sketching football-themed creations at an early age. As a child growing up in Philadelphia, he would read up on cities and countries near and far before making jersey and crest designs to pass the time.

From the get-go, imagination and flair were key parts of his approach, and that has continued to this day, allowing him to realize all sorts of concepts for teams from a myriad of backgrounds. “We design shirts with fans of a club in mind rather than players. And fans are increasingly looking for creative designs to wear, whether that be for pick-up games in the park or music festivals.

“I think part of the appeal comes from the colours and designs used on football kits. They’re often a lot more creative and out-there than traditional men’s clothing, so football shirts offer something different. They’re also comfortable, so they fit in with the growing trend towards athleisure,” Robby explains.

Indeed, football jerseys are very in today; whether it’s the new releases by the top clubs or the retro classic continually making a comeback, there is a lot of demand for eye-catching sportswear.

Icarus Football’s jerseys appeal to a wide audience because they are steeped in personality, unique designs, and more. As Robby explains, the shirts they make are inspired by each club’s “history, iconography, imagery, fan culture, location”, offering an antidote to the bland factory-manufactured shirts that clubs and fans are often forced to buy.

Robby and his team offer distinctive, eye-catching shirts that clubs can wear with pride when they take to the field. Fans, too, can appreciate the carnival of colour that defines many of their creations, the tailored detail of the pieces, and the thoughtful artistry, too.

“For us, a design that references a team’s culture and history makes a shirt special. But for it to be totally iconic–it needs to be worn in an interesting context.

“The Holland ’88 and Germany ’90 jerseys are two of the most iconic designs of all time, and deservedly so. They’re amazing designs. But if they weren’t worn by those trophy-winning teams and wrapped up in those historic moments, I don’t think they would be considered as legendary as they are.

“The moments in which shirts are worn and the players that wear them both contribute to the status of a shirt. That also speaks a little bit as to why retro shirts have become so popular.

“Legendary players from the 80s/90s seem cooler, perhaps because a lot of young people didn’t get to watch them play during their careers. Only getting to watch legends like [Gheorge] Hagi, [Marco] Van Basten, [Johan] Cruyff, [Michael] Laudrup, [Roberto] Baggio …through limited YouTube videos and highlight reels makes them appear all the more legendary. And that rubs off a bit on the status of the shirts that they wore.”

Robbie’s thoughts confirm the notion that retro jerseys have long been on the comeback trail.

Instagram is full of posts with throwbacks to iconic shirts of old – and to football’s traditions and magical teams. Boca Juniors, Fiorentina, Liverpool, AC Milan, Paris Saint-Germain, Barcelona, and more are just some of the clubs that feature heavily in posts dripping with charm, style, and those-were-the-days vibes.

After all, what football fan can scroll past a post of Diego Maradona in the pomp of his career wearing that special Mars-sponsored Napoli shirt without leaving an emphatic ‘like’?

Nostalgia is a big art of the apparent resurgence in popularity of retro replicas, but kit designer Robbie also believes retro shirts are popular because of something else, too “Retro shirts are baggier and made from materials that are almost closer to modern-day sweatshirts than football shirts. That plays well when it comes to fashion.”

Indeed, Icarus Football’s line of historical concept jerseys speaks to how sought-after retro-style kits are. “We really love working on our historical jersey range. We love history, and these jerseys are playful attempts at football shirts for bygone civilizations (e.g., Ancient Egypt, Mesopotamia, The Republic of Venice, The Mongol Empire). There’s so much content to use as inspiration for these designs.”

New Amsterdam FC and Louisiana Krewe are two clubs Icarus FC have worked with in recent times, and they have also worked with clubs in the Ghana Premier League, among so many others. For several years, they have provided a nonconformist approach to fashioning beautiful jerseys shining with distinction. So, what about the future – what teams would Robby and his crew like to work with?

“At a top, top level, it would have to be a national team that’s open to something creative and experimental. National sides have so much imagery, history, and iconography that can be used for the purposes of a personal design. As a geography nerd, I’m extremely interested in working with national sides off the beaten path.

“I’d get just as much joy out of creating a design for Belize as for Brazil. Same thing goes for clubs. Give me TP Mazembe in the Congo, FC Noah in Armenia, and FC Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia (just to name a few) and I’d be a happy man.”

#2573. U21 European Championship Final: English Manipulation of the German Pressing – MH

von Next Generation am 06.07.2025 in den Kategorien National Teams mit 1 Kommentar

England wins the U21 European Championship final against Germany 3-2. After just 20 minutes, England leads 2-0. This aspect analysis focuses on the reasons behind the German attacking press’s lack of access to England’s build-up play.

The U21 European Championship final offered several interesting tactical elements. This analysis focuses on Germany’s lack of access in their attacking pressing and marking. Particularly in the first half, England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press, often gaining large amounts of space in the final third, which led to dangerous scoring opportunities.

The early deficit also contributed to Germany being unable to focus, as they usually do, on securing depth in their pressing. Instead, they were forced to put direct pressure on the ball carrier in order to force turnovers. After the equalizer to make it 2-2, Germany noticeably pressed high less frequently. Therefore, this analysis examines Germany’s pressing and marking, as well as England’s build-up play, up to the 60th minute.

One of the trends at the U21 European Championship was that many teams aimed to press the opponent’s goal kicks with a +1 player on the last line or in the space between the lines just in front of the back line. Many teams—including Germany—used man-oriented marking when closing down during goal kicks.

Since most teams build up from a 1-4-2-4 structure on goal kicks, it is equally common to press man-to-man from a 4-1-3-2 shape, with the two holding midfielders (the “sixes”) staggered vertically.

The deeper-lying holding midfielder (for Germany: Martel) acts as the +1 player, positioning himself in space based on the location of the ball. When the opponent plays through the space between the lines, he can create a numerical advantage there. In the final third, pressing is carried out against a 1-4-2 build-up using a 3-2 shape. The more advanced holding midfielder (for Germany: Reitz) typically positions himself centrally and marks the ball-near holding midfielder, while the far-side winger presses the ball-far holding midfielder.

The English side, by contrast, caused problems for the German team’s marking assignments through an asymmetrical structure. As a result, England had several options for exploiting their numerical superiority in the build-up without having to immediately play into the space between the lines.

What remained consistent was the intention to establish central possession in front of the first pressing line using different players, in order to build up play on either side. Central possession makes it more difficult for the pressing team to steer the play in a specific direction, as the passing angles from central areas are wider than those from more advanced or wider positions.

Central possession complicates the opponent’s shaping of play. Anderson’s drop frees him from Woltemade’s marking shadow and creates a numerical advantage against Nebel, who must now cover both the advanced full-back and Anderson.

The asymmetry in England’s build-up play also allowed them to repeatedly exploit their numerical superiority in specific areas tailored to Germany’s pressing structure. By stretching the positioning of their two holding midfielders (the “sixes”), Reitz was forced to cover too much ground to mark both or to shift quickly to the ball-near midfielder.

Because Germany, for the reasons mentioned above, struggled to steer the press in a specific direction, Reitz was also unable to position himself closer to the ball-near player during goal kicks. Instead, he was forced to choose which of the two midfielders to mark man-to-man.

The wide, asymmetric positioning of the holding midfielders and advanced full-backs makes both midfielders available for passes, forcing Reitz to choose whom to mark. German forwards can’t shadow the opposing midfielders, while German wingers must decide between marking the spaced-out midfielders or full-backs.

England’s positional rotations during build-up play after goal kicks were most often initiated by holding midfielder Anderson. When Germany applied pressure (as shown in the diagram above), Anderson would frequently drop into the right half-space, almost into a right-sided centre-back position, while fellow holding midfielder Scott positioned himself more centrally, and No. 10 McAtee dropped into the higher left half-space.

When Anderson instead dropped centrally in front of the goalkeeper, the right centre-back would shift wide, which in turn affected the positioning of other central players and full-backs. The specific rotations of the key players, including their reference points and triggers, are discussed in more detail in the section on England’s build-up against Germany’s high pressing.

A key aspect of England’s build-up against Germany’s pressing was their ability to evade pressure through these rotations. Since Germany used man-oriented marking, they followed the English players during these movements, which repeatedly opened up spaces that England could then exploit. For example, when McAtee dropped deep into the far-side half-space, it pulled Martel—who was defending space-oriented in the center—out of position.

The aim was to repeatedly open up central areas by drawing German players out of the middle. When the full-backs, due to the rotations, were positioned deep and wide in possession, the ball-near holding midfielder would shift outward, thereby opening the central channel. This would often be followed by an overlapping run by the full-back into the half-space, allowing him to be found deep in the center with his marker behind him and plenty of space to operate.

Luring central players out of position and opening up space through rotations is one of the core principles of England’s build-up play. It significantly disrupted Germany’s ability to gain access through their man-marking approach during pressing.

Holding midfielder Anderson’s run outward opens the center, which can then be exploited by the full-back’s typical forward run.

England also added flexibility by repeatedly using long balls from their build-up play. Especially when both the full-backs and the holding midfielders were positioned deep, they opted for long passes as soon as Germany’s wingers and central players were lured far enough out. The 2–0 goal resulted from one such long ball, which was held up by striker Stansfield and laid off to the advancing Elliott and McAtee in the half-space, who now had plenty of room to operate in the open central area.

Although these long balls weren’t always as successful as in the lead-up to the 2–0, they had the effect of preventing Germany from pressing too aggressively, as players had to remain ready to cover depth in case of another long ball. For example, Martel pushed forward only hesitantly toward the dropping No. 10 McAtee, giving him significantly more time on the ball in central areas.

Against man-oriented marking systems, it is particularly important to apply intense pressure on the ball carrier, since progression is otherwise easier than against a zonal setup.

As described, England repeatedly managed to exploit their numerical advantage in the build-up. However, Germany’s pressing approach also contributed to their lack of access. The primary aim of Germany’s pressing when closing down is less about disrupting the build-up itself, and more about winning the ball in a way that immediately creates a transition opportunity.

To do so, Germany tries to use its forwards to immediately block passing lanes to the flanks, forcing the play through the third man or central passes.

Recovering possession through intercepting a pass has the advantage over winning a tackle in that it tends to allow better control of the ball and therefore more often leads to a transition opportunity. Additionally, central ball recoveries naturally result in a shorter route to goal and, statistically, in higher-quality chances in front of goal.

However, this type of pressing also means less pressure is placed on the ball carrier, since the focus is on directing play and winning the ball after a pass. As a result, England’s ball carriers had more time to locate the free +1 player, made available through asymmetry and rotations.

In hindsight, it might have been more effective to place greater emphasis on actively disrupting the build-up itself, because England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press dangerously. At the same time, Germany had the ability to control the game through their own possession, so it wasn’t absolutely necessary to rely on winning the ball high up the pitch to create chances.

Germany’s attacking pressing operated on principles similar to those of their closing down (Zustellen). From a 4-4-2 formation with a slightly advanced Reitz on the left half-space, the forwards aimed to channel the opponent’s build-up play out wide in order to isolate the wide build-up players and engage them in man-to-man marking.

On the last defensive line, Germany aimed to maintain a +1 numerical advantage, which is why the far-side holding midfielder was usually responsible for covering depth. The German wingers were expected to track back from the full-backs to press the half-backs in the three-man defensive line that frequently formed.

Even when applying attacking pressing from open play, Germany was rarely able to gain effective access to England’s build-up. This was primarily due to England’s positional play during build-up. England’s main objective in possession is to lure opponents out of position and then exploit the spaces that open up. This goal is achieved through positional rotations that make it especially difficult for the opponent to apply effective pressure on the ball carrier during pressing. The frequency of these rotations strongly resembles the rotation-heavy positional play famously associated with Paris Saint-Germain.

The following outlines the key running paths, rotations, and reference points of the most important players.

The center-backs were rarely involved in the rotations. Only when one of the holding midfielders dropped into the build-up line did the center-backs position themselves wider. Likewise, striker Stansfield provided a fixed presence in the central deep-lying position.

Most rotations initially originated from the holding midfielders, particularly Anderson. Most frequently, he dropped into the right half-space just ahead of the center-backs. This caused the right full-back to position wider and winger Elliott to drop deeper into the half-space at the level of the last defensive line. As a result, Woltemade and Nebel had to press two players, creating a 3 vs. 2 overload.

There were also occasions when Anderson dropped into the central center-back position. Consequently, the full-backs rotated into the half-spaces, or No. 10 McAtee dropped deeper. Notably, Anderson could be found almost anywhere on the pitch. At times, he overloaded the far side, which was then followed by a role swap between him and holding midfielder Scott.

Holding midfielder Scott often positioned himself in spaces that were left vacant after a sequence of rotations. Usually, Scott remained central or rotated roles with holding midfielder Anderson. It also happened that Scott took up an open full-back position when both the winger and the full-back rotated deep.

A particularly noticeable tendency of both holding midfielders was that, when in possession, they rotated toward the flank if a wide player was positioned close to the first build-up line, making themselves available along the sideline. This had the advantage of stretching the center even further.

This was especially important because England frequently won second balls after losing possession in build-up play. In the resulting transition situation, the central area was completely free, leading to several dangerous counter-attacks through the now open middle of the pitch.

Livramento, as the right full-back, primarily oriented himself around Anderson and the right winger Elliott. In relation to Elliott, Livramento always behaved in a complementary manner: when one occupied the wide position, the other took up the half-space. It was also common for Livramento to invert and drop into the deeper half-space, with Elliott moving wider in response, and vice versa.

Anderson served as a secondary reference point. Whenever Anderson dropped back to form a wide back three, Livramento either moved inverted or stayed wide and deep. If Anderson remained central, Livramento positioned himself near the center-backs in the half-space, from where he could rotate forward into depth if the outside lane was free.

On the left side, full-back Hinshelwood and winger Hutchinson rotated according to the same principles as Livramento and Elliott. Hinshelwood also frequently inverted into the deeper half-space or moved wide and deep. Both full-backs, Livramento and Hinshelwood, often initiated rotations through their inverted runs when the ball was with the near-side build-up player.

Runs into depth, however, were usually triggered only when other players moved to offer passing options. The No. 10 McAtee also played an important role as a reference point. When McAtee (and/or Hutchinson) moved into the left half-space, Hinshelwood rotated oppositely into depth.

McAtee, as a left-sided No. 10, had a freer role. He oriented himself around the holding midfielders to occupy or overload the central area when needed. He also rotated positions with left winger Hutchinson. Often, McAtee initially moved far into the left half-space to pull defenders out of the No. 10 zone behind him and then sometimes rotated further back toward the central center-back position.

In response, either full-back Hinshelwood or holding midfielder Anderson rotated forward into depth. Alternatively, winger Hutchinson could rotate into the half-space, prompting full-back Hinshelwood to rotate wider.

The English rotations created difficult conditions for Germany’s man-oriented attacking pressing. Man-marking was repeatedly manipulated, which in turn stretched and opened up spaces. Thanks to the flexibility of long balls and superiority in second balls, England’s build-up play additionally benefited in the first half. This led to repeated situations resembling counter-attacks, as England had plenty of central space available after bypassing the press.

The early goal also forced Germany to press higher more frequently and reduced their tendency to drop deep. Germany’s pressing behavior against England’s build-up thus became one of the decisive factors influencing the course of the game in the first half.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. Of course, the book from Spielverlagerung.de is not missing. For MH, football is not just a game, it’s a way of life. He can be found on X under Mh_sv5 and LinkedIn.

#2572. C.J. Stroud keeps Texans' playoff hopes alive; CFB Week 12 picks; NBA's biggest disappointments

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

The NBA season started one month ago today. The first stanza of the campaign brought a great deal of excitement at the top of the league with superstars doing superstar things and most of the projected championship contenders getting off to hot starts. But we also saw injuries, a disappointing first handful of games from Mikal Bridges and an Eastern Conference that is not nearly as dominant as it was supposed to be.

Those are three of the biggest letdowns of the young season. Here's our John Gonzalez on why Bridges might be the greatest dud of any individual player:

Another major disappointment: The Kings. How can a team underperform expectations when those expectations are already about as low as they come? Well, Sacramento sure has found a way. With a 1-13 record and after a puzzling trade, the Kings earned their spot in our ranking of the NBA's most hopeless teams.

The College Football Selection Committee is in love with the SEC. Only one time in three different rankings have the bracket-makers ranked a team from that conference lower than AP Top 25 voters. Whether or not you think it's fair, the numbers largely back it up. In fact, two-loss No. 5 Texas even has a better resume score than undefeated No. 2 Utah! So maybe the committee is not all that out of line. You can be sure they will have their eyes on these five key matchups in Week 12.

Another important clash is the only top-25 contest of the week: No. 1 Georgia at No. 21 South Carolina. In his Six Pack of picks, our Tom Fornelli explained why the Bulldogs will roll on the road.

Moving away from the SEC, look out for a potential upset in the Big Ten. Nothing is going well for Michigan, but the Wolverines are only small underdogs against unbeaten No. 4 UCLA. These five factors will determine whether the Bruins move one step closer to the CFP or fall for the first time this season.

Here's how to watch the biggest games of Week 12 and our picks for each of them:

This is easily the most lopsided week of the NFL season. The Bills and Chiefs are three-score favorites. The Bears and Broncos are also favored by double digits. The Cowboys, Lions, Jaguars and Bengals are all favored by about a touchdown. You know how these things go, though. One of these favorites is bound to lose. We put a few of them on upset alert, and a handful of our experts are in agreement that the Lions are among the most vulnerable.

First of all, the Buccaneers have just as much to play for as the Lions. Both of them are locked into tightly contested division battles. The motivation will be there for a Tampa Bay team that could somehow sneak into the playoffs even with a losing record. And then there's the Tampa Bay defense, which has forced at least four turnovers in each of its last three games. Our Tyler Sullivan said it would not surprise him if Jared Goff's interception streak continues.

And even though our Jordan Dajani could not bring himself to pick the upset outright, he does see the Buccaneers keeping this one highly competitive.

#2571. Victor Wembanyama has dunked so much he hurt his hand, so he came up with a unique solution: The 'shunk'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Remember at the end of Space Jam, when Michael Jordan launched himself off of the butt of a MonStar to dunk from the half-court line? Well, imagine the exact opposite of that play. Instead of an impossibly long dunk, Thursday night's NBA action gave us an impossibly short jumper.

Let's set the stage here. The San Antonio Spurs are leading the Los Angeles Clippers by 12 points with under four minutes remaining. Victor Wembanyama is alone under the basket. He led the NBA with 71 dunks on the season to that point. Nobody else, as of the beginning of play Thursday, had reached even 50. But Wembanyama does not take this opportunity to slam down dunk No. 72, at least not intentionally. No, San Antonio's Martian with an eight-foot wingspan jumps directly in front of the basket... and flicks his wrist downward in what was seemingly a shooting motion. It swishes through the rim. Two points.

Did Wemby just... shoot it from above the rim??? 🤯😲 pic.twitter.com/1YDxy8mwy8

Officially, it will count as dunk No. 72 on the season for Wembanyama. Unofficially, as coined by Spurs broadcaster Sean Elliott, it was the first "shunk" of his season. Or, well, perhaps anyone's. It takes a perfect storm of circumstances to create a shunk: an uncommonly large basketball player, a lane open enough to ensure no defensive resistance, and perhaps rarest of all, a center disinterested in dunking.

That begs an important question: what compelled this maneuver? Well, as is so often the case, necessity was the mother of invention.

Wembanyama has a blister on his right hand. He doesn't know when exactly it came, but he knows where it came from. "It definitely came from dunking a lot," he told reporters after the game Thursday. The math here checks out. Wembanyama dunked 178 times in 64 games last season. That's around 2.8 dunks per game. Even if we discount the shunk, he's at 71 dunks through 16 games this season, or around 4.4.

Fortunately for the Spurs, Wembanyama has no plans to stop dunking, "but if I can avoid it, I would," he said after the win. The blister, according to Wembanyama, is quite painful. You'd hardly know it from watching him play. Wembanyama is averaging career-highs in points, rebounds, blocks and field goal percentage thus far this season. He is leading a 13-3 Spurs team that is tied for the NBA's best record thus far, and along with Luka Dončić, he is one of the two heavy favorites to win this season's MVP award.

If he's looking for a fringe benefit here, the "shunk" might save him from the "run and just dunk" esque criticism that Giannis Antetokounmpo recevied during his MVP pursuits. This is genuine innovation in the short-distance conversion space. Innovation is rarely in short supply in San Antonio. Earlier this week, Wembanyama threw himself multiple passes off of the backboard in a single quarter. Every time you turn on a Spurs game, there's a real chance Wembanyama does something you've never seen before, and the shunk is no exception.

#2570. Drake Maye out indefinitely with fibula: Big picture questions now facing Patriots offseason, beyond

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There are still seven games left on the schedule, but New England's season unofficially and unceremoniously ended in the aftermath of Week 10. That's due to Drake Maye suffering a broken fibula, which will sideline him deep into the regular season if not for the whole year. The Patriots' chances of returning to the playoffs after a surprise run to the Super Bowl a year ago are all but out the window.

The team enters its Week 11 bye at 5-5 and is slotted as the No. 8 seed in the conference. With Maye on the shelf and Tommy DeVito poised to start the rest of the way (unless they add a free agent), the second half could be tough sledding for Mike Vrabel's team. That's especially true in December, when they'll have a three-week stretch against the Bills, Vikings, and Chiefs. Even with Maye in the fold, those were going to be tough matchups to overcome. Without their star franchise quarterback, they're borderline insurmountable.

Really, this injury to Maye changes the lens through which we need to view the Patriots. The focus shifts away from the nitty-gritty of the regular season and possible playoff position to the bigger-picture, existential topics that extend beyond 2026. Below, we'll highlight some of the ripple effects of Maye's injury, along with other pressing questions facing the franchise as they look to bounce back in 2027 with their star QB in the fold.

One element of Maye's injury that is worth highlighting is that it comes at a less-than-ideal time for the quarterback, who becomes extension-eligible this offseason. It's hard to imagine this injury truly derailing any sort of negotiation between Maye's camp and the Patriots front office. That said, you can't really rule it out either.

That's especially true considering Maye could be—and should be—looking to reset the market at the position. After all, he already has an MVP runner-up and a Super Bowl appearance on his résumé. That means exceeding Patrick Mahomes' $64 million-per-season rate that he recently inked with the Kansas City Chiefs. And that's on the low end, as other quarterbacks like Caleb Williams and/or C.J. Stroud could balloon that market-setting figure this offseason with their looming extensions.

When you're talking about executing the largest contract in NFL history, there could be some trepidation depending on how Maye's ankle recovers. The Patriots have also historically been known to drag out talks, most recently not signing Christian Gonzalez to his market-setting deal until just before the start of the regular season. While waiting with Maye could give them further clarity on how his ankle heals, it also runs the risk of the price going up as other QBs sign their deals.

Drake Maye has also looked like two completely different quarterbacks over the course of this season. Through the first three games of the season, Maye was in the midst of an all-time-bad Super Bowl hangover. New England got off to a 1-2 start that saw the third-year quarterback throw six interceptions and put up the league's lowest quarterback rating of 58.6. Since then, though, Maye looked closer to last year's MVP-caliber run despite the Patriots' litany of injuries. Between Weeks 4 and 10, Maye ranked third in touchdown passes (17), fifth in completion percentage over expectation (plus-4.2%), second in success rate (51.1%), third in EPA per dropback (0.20), and second in yards per attempt (8.9) among 31 qualified quarterbacks, all while being bressured at the fourth-highest rate in the league (43.6%).

Possibly intertwined with Maye's extension could come some hard questions regarding who stays and who goes on this current version of the Patriots roster.

For instance, this offseason New England has receiver DeMario Douglas, offensive lineman Greg Van Roten, offensive lineman Michael Onwenu, safety Kevin Byard, linebacker Christian Elliss, and receiver Mack Hollins, all set to hit free agency. On top of that group, corner Carlton Davis (would create $16.5 million in cap space if cut), pass rusher Harold Landry ($14.5 million), and right tackle Morgan Mosses ($9 million) are all potential cut candidates to clear up space.

Each of those players mentioned is, or at least has been, a key contributor to the on-field product. Hollins and Douglas are the last two receivers on the roster who meaningfully contributed to the Patriots' 2024 Super Bowl Run; Onwenu has been New England's most reliable offensive lineman over the last few years; Byard currently leads the team in interceptions, while Ellis leads the team in tackles. New England will need to either look to the draft to fill those holes or dip their toe into the free-agent market.

At the moment, Over the Cap projects the Patriots to have roughly $16.8 million in available cap space.

There's really no other way to describe the A.J. Brown trade than as an utter disaster. When the Patriots shipped out a 2028 first-round pick as part of the blockbuster trade to acquire the star receiver, Brown was supposed to be the crown jewel that would take New England's offense to a new level. That hasn't materialized.

Brown has been limited to four games due to an array of injuries. He suffered a high ankle sprain early in the season, in the opening matchup against the Seattle Seahawks. That forced him on injured reserve. Then, after just two games back, a knee injury forced him to miss the club's Week 8 and Week 9 contests. To make matters even more maddening with Brown, he sufferd a third injury, leaving Sunday's Week 10 loss to the Lions early with a hamstring injury that will force him to miss multiple weeks.

So far, the wideout has suited up in four games and caught 11 of his 26 targets for 128 yards and zero touchdowns. Brown has also had three drops.

With Maye sidelined for the year, Brown faces immense pressure to produce when he's back on the field in 2027 and make last summer's sizable investment worth it. That could be a true roll of the dice, as Brown will be entering his age-30 season in 2027 and with a sizable injury history. He may not be the player he was during his early days in Tennessee or at the peak of his tenure in Philadelphia, but the Patriots will need more than what they've gotten from him next year.

If they don't, their record will likely suffer because of it and make that 2028 first-round pick that'll be awarded to the Eagles as part of the trade even more valuable.

While Drake Maye is still just 24 years old and hasn't even stepped into his prime yet, his team will be at a crossroads next year. The core they've built around Maye faces a make-or-break season that could lead to a reset if things continue to trend in the wrong direction.

For example, A.J. Brown is signed through 2029, but has no guaranteed money remaining on his contract in 2028 and 2029. If he doesn't turn a corner next year, it'd be hard to imagine New England re-upping him, and they would likely try to move on to clear space. Free-agent acquisition and fellow wideout Romeo Doubs is in the same boat as Brown. Those are two integral pieces to the offense that could be out the door quicker than they came in, and leave the organization looking for new pieces to surround Maye with, albeit now while paying him top dollar.

With the team not owning their own first-round pick in 2028 either, it only stresses the importance of these players (and others like them on the roster) finding their footing, as no blue-chippers are around the corner if they should struggle again in 2027.

#2569. Damian Lillard stars in his Milwaukee return in another stark reminder of how bleak things are for the Bucks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

MILWAUKEE -- "Stay up! Stay up!" The pleading voice of the Milwaukee Bucks' in-arena host was still echoing around a half-empty Fiserv Forum early on Thursday night when Damian Lillard knocked the ball away from Tyler Herro and coasted the other way for the first points of a 124-114 Portland Trail Blazers victory.

Bucks fans are supposed to stay standing until their team scores. Those who are still proud enough to show up and follow the tradition get much more time on their feet than they did when Lillard was still in a Bucks jersey. They waited nearly two minutes on Thursday, then spent the next two hours watching Lillard pour in a season-high 33 points to send the Bucks to their 12th consecutive defeat and an NBA-worst 1-15 record.

Lillard's return to the court where he tore his Achilles a little more than a year ago -- which came just one night after the Bucks faced Giannis Antetokounmpo for the first time -- was yet another reminder of how wrong things have gone in Milwaukee over the last few years, and the grim future the franchise faces. Jrue Holiday's 22 points, seven assists and four steals on Thursday only added to the misery.

Trail Blazers coach Micah Nori joked pre-game that this might be the "first and only revenge game" of Lillard's career. Afterward, Lillard, who was waived by Milwaukee mere weeks after his injury, downplayed its significance. It was just a normal game, he said, "other than it just being the first time that I've played on the court since I got hurt."

Lillard's aggressiveness may have suggested otherwise, but both he and Nori attributed his approach to the Blazers being without Deni Avdija and Ja Morant. "When you're down your next two top scorers, I knew that I would need to be a little more assertive," Lillard said.

No one knew what to expect from the 36-year-old Lillard this season after such an extended layoff, but through 15 games he's averaging 20.9 points and 4.1 assists, and shooting 35.8% from 3-point range.

"He still has the stop and go, which has made him so effective. Obviously, the jumper and his legs. I think the biggest difference would be, 18 months without playing, I don't know if you want to call it rust or timing, that's the only thing you see," Nori said pre-game. "And it's coming back. Every single day, you can see it. But when you're playing against the best athletes in the world, the best players in the world, the best defenders in the world, it is gonna take you a little bit of time to get back up to speed. But as far as from a health standpoint, you really wouldn't know it."

The moment Lillard's Achilles snapped 572 days ago during Game 4 of a first-round playoff series against the Indiana Pacers, everyone knew it was a turning point for the Bucks. But no one could have foreseen everything that's happened since then.

The Bucks waived Lillard not even two months after the injury and stretched the remaining $113 million on his contract over five years in order to create the cap space to sign Myles Turner to a four-year, $107 million deal with a player option for the 2028-29 season.

"I thought it was pretty simple. I was injured. I wasn't gonna be available to play last season, and the team was focused on bringing somebody in here that they could pair with Giannis so that they could still be a competitive team, which is the business side of it," Lillard said Thursday morning at shootaround. "I saw it for what it was, and I moved on."

The desperate ploy to keep Antetokounmpo happy didn't work. Now, both he and Lillard are gone, while Turner is averaging just 7.1 points and six rebounds on 36.2% shooting this season and the Bucks are still paying Lillard $22,516,603 each year through 2030. If you break that figure down by game, they gave Lillard $247,592 for the trouble of beating them on Thursday while Turner sat and watched with a shoulder injury.

Five years ago, Antetokounmpo and Holiday were carrying the Larry O'Brien trophy through the streets of Milwaukee. Three years ago, Holiday was traded for Lillard. Just over a year ago, Lillard tore his Achilles in the most recent playoff game at Fiserv Forum and was waived. Now, Antetokounmpo is leading the 9-6 Miami Heat, who sit in fourth place in the Eastern Conference, while Holiday and Lillard are together in the same backcourt for the 10-5 Trail Blazers, who occupy sixth in the Western Conference.

And the Bucks, who haven't won a playoff series since 2022 and don't own their own first-round pick until 2031, the year after they'll stop paying Lillard? They're 1-15, have the worst record in the league and are in the midst of the second-longest losing streak in franchise history. Oh, and they're also under investigation for salary cap circumvention relating to Gary Trent Jr.'s $64 million contract.

No team has a bleaker present or future than the Bucks.

Just how bad are the vibes in Milwaukee? Major Goolsby's, a sports bar down the street from the arena, has started running a new promotion on game nights: everything's free if the Bucks win.

#2568. Daniel Jones released by Colts: Why QB's contract almost ensures he'll clear waivers, be free agent

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Daniel Jones era in Indianapolis didn't make it to the end of Year 2. The Colts cut their run with the veteran quarterback short, waiving him in the aftermath of a 26-3 defeat at the hands of the Houston Texans in Week 11.

While cutting ties at this juncture was shocking for the Colts, a divorce seemed inevitable this offseason as the team is 3-8 with Jones as a main culprit of the organization's shortcomings. His 15 turnovers are the most in the NFL, and his 13 interceptions set a new career-high. Thursday's loss was also his sixth straight game with an interception, which is the longest streak by a Colts player since Curtis Painter in 2011.

That's not the version of Jones the Colts were hoping to get when they signed him to a two-year, $88 million contract extension back in March. They had hoped Jones would return to the player he was over the first eight games of the 2025 season, prior to suffering a season-ending Achilles tear. Over that stretch, Jones had the Colts at 7-1 while boasting a 109.5 passer rating. However, that flash in the pan was just that. Jones was unable to recapture that magic, and Indianapolis is now left paying a hefty price.

Below, we'll explain some financial ramifications regarding the Colts waiving Jones, what his contract says and why it'd be extremely surprising for a team to claim him before he clears waivers on Monday.

For 2027, the final year of Jones' extension, the quarterback was set to have a $46.8 million cap hit. By waiving him, Indy will actually clear about $11.6 million in space for this offseason as they look for a new signal-caller and replenish the roster. While there are cap savings, Jones will account for $35.2 million in dead money, which is tied to his $44 million signing bonus that was prorated through 2030, according to CBS Sports salary cap expert Joel Corry.

Again, this is assuming Jones is waived, which he almost certainly will be (we explain why below).

Meanwhile, Spotrac notes that Indy will have paid out $49.8 million to Jones for 11 games this season. Ouch.

Jones is now subject to waivers until Monday at 4 p.m. ET. Any team in the league can put in a claim for the veteran quarterback, but it's highly unlikely that'll be the case. Why? Any team that claims Jones would take on $2 million for the rest of this season and $38 million in non-guaranteed money in 2027, as noted by NFL Network.

When it comes to 2027, $6.5 million of Jones' base salary and a $4 million roster bonus are guaranteed for injury. So, any team claiming him off of waivers would be on the hook for at least $10.5 million next season.

It would be downright shocking to see any club electing to go down that route in a pursuit of Jones at this stage. If they're interested, the more cost-effective move would be for hiim to clear waivers, have the Colts pick up the tab, and sign him as a free agent at a lower number. Then, the hypothetical new team would only be responsible for whatever it signs him for.
