#2565. NBA One-Month Superlatives: MVP, top rookie, best surprise and fresh title predictions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Memphis Grizzlies pounded the Golden State Warriors on Thursday to move to 12-4 on the year. The Grizzlies were a popular pick to surprise some folks this year, but nobody saw this coming. On the other hand, Luka Dončić and Victor Wembanyama are lording over the league like castles on a hill, and that wasn't so hard to predict.

And then there's been everything in between. All the injuries, perhaps most notably. The Raptors and Pacers entered the season being hyped as new-look contenders, but so far Tyrese Haliburton and Kawhi Leonard have combined to play six games. The Warriors went from an eight-game winning streak to the Washington Generals with one Stephen Curry abdominal tweak. The 76ers can't lose a clutch game in a maze. Paul George has been reborn in Boston. The Rockets are flying. The Heat are getting hot. The Knicks' fog is lifting. It feels like Damian Lillard never left the Blazers. This rookie class looks potentially historic.

So much has happened over the first month of the season that we're going to pause for a moment, take stock of what we've seen, and hand out a few bits of early hardware. Who's been the MVP so far? What about the best rookie? What has been the biggest surprise? Biggest disappointment? In light of what we've seen so far, is anyone ready to change their preseason Finals pick? Our staff took a collective shot at tackling these topics below.

Botkin: It's a two-horse race so far and nobody is going to argue much with either pick, but I'm going with Luka. I thought the Lakers would be good (their over/under 46.5 win total was way too low), but not tied-for-the-best-record-in-the-league good. Likewise, we all knew Luka would score huge, but not damn-near 40 PPG huge. Throw in north of seven assists and seven rebounds and almost two steals a night, and the numbers are simply too overwhelming to deny.

Gonzalez: This is really tough. Luka Dončić has been playing some of the best basketball of his career, and he's a huge reason why the Lakers are down as my big surprise over the first month of the season. But for as good as Luka has been, Wemby's two-way dominance gives him the edge here. Wembanyama had the second 50-point game of his career against the Mavs, and he's averaging a 28-point double-double on 53% shooting from the field. He's also blocking an outrageous 4.1 shots per game and averaging more than a steal per outing. There's no answer for him at either end of the floor.

Kalland: Wemby's been awesome but for the first month it's gotta be Luka. He's averaging 38 points per game on 47/38/86 splits! The Lakers are 13-3 in spite of defensive concerns, and it's because Dončić is out of his mind. What's amazing is he's going to have to keep up this ridiculous pace to win MVP and for the Lakers to remain at the top of the West. I'm excited to see how long he can maintain this level.

Maloney: I won't argue with anyone who picks Luka Dončić when he's averaging nearly 40 points per game, but I'm going with Wembanyama because of his two-way dominance. He's third in scoring, fourth in rebounding and first in blocks by a significant margin. The 1.7 blocks-per-game gap between Wembanyama (3.9) and Donovan Clingan (2.2), who sits in second, is as big as the gap between Clingan and Dean Wade (0.5), who ranks 102nd in the league. In 483 minutes with Wembanyama on the floor this season, the Spurs have a 98.7 defensive rating; in 290 minutes without him, they have a 123.4 defensive rating. Overall, Wembanyama has an unfathomable +41.5 net rating differential.

Quinn: Dončić is flirting with 40 points per game. He's leading the NBA in both 3-point attempts and free throws. He's the undisputed engine of the NBA's best offense, one that dies whenever he rests. The Lakers have the NBA's best record because Luka Dončić is on their team. That's it. They're average at basically everything else: rebounding, defense, you name it. But their offense dominates because he is on their team. Victor Wembanyama has much more to work with around him. No one else is even in their galaxy, though Stephen Curry might've had a case had he stayed healthy.

Salerno: I've been pleasantly surprised with the Lakers so far. The pieces are working together nicely. However, the Lakers obviously wouldn't obvousuly be this good without Dončić, who is somehow taking his game to an entirely new level. He's on a mission to win MVP. He's been the best player in the league for the first month of the season. I think this will be the year he finally wins the award.

Botkin: I actually think Darius Acuff's numbers are actually too good in the sense that voters can't fathom a rookie averaging 26 and 7 without it being some fishy gimmick. It's not a gimmick. He just has total control of an NBA offense, which would make any player's numbers go up, Luka Dončić included. That said, Lendeborg has been better as both a real go-to player on a real team and from a scoring efficiency standpoint. The honeymoon has been heavily interrupted with Stephen Curry's injury as the Warriors look, well, like the Kings. But as of now Lendeborg deserves the award. Long term, I'm really watching Darryn Peterson as Utah's season quickly circles the drain. His numbers are rising quickly, and it may not be long before his development becomes Utah's undisputed top priority.

Gonzalez: Lendeborg picked a fight with Luka in his very first game as a pro, trash-talked while guarding the Lakers superstar, then said he lost all respect for him afterward. He stepped into the starting lineup and immediately looked like he belonged for an injury-plagued Warriors team that sorely needed his presence. And he was so unnerved by a blowout loss to the Spurs that he chopped off his hair, leaving Steve Kerr to tell the media "apparently that's his response to getting beat by 40, is to go right to the barber." His personality alone wins him the award. The numbers are good, too.

Kalland: This rookie class has lived up to the hype so far, but right now I have to give the edge to the Warriors rookie sensation. Lendeborg came into the league talking that talk, and while he's put his foot in his mouth here and there, he's largely walked the walk to back it up. What separates him from the likes of Darius Acuff and Cameron Boozer currently is his combination of productivity and efficiency. But we've already seen that take a dip without Stephen Curry so there is certainly an opportunity for others to make up ground as the Warriors struggle without their top star.

Maloney: Lendeborg has started to fade a bit, and so have the Warriors since Steph Curry went down with an oblique injury, but the No. 11 pick has still done enough to earn the nod ahead of Darius Acuff and Cameron Boozer. Everyone liked the Lendeborg pick for the Warriors, but no one expected this. He's come in and immediately established himself as their second-best player while doing a little bit of everything. He's second among rookies in scoring, second in rebounding, fifth in assists and tied for fourth in steals, all while shooting 37.2% from 3-point range.

Quinn: Cameron Boozer is probably trending toward winning. His 3-point shooting is coming around, his interior scoring is progressing, and he does all of the little things everyone promised. Darius Acuff has the biggest numbers, but they're fake. Not fake in the empty calories sense, but fake in that all of the other rookies are being asked to play roles on real basketball teams, whereas Sacramento has elected to devote its entire season to Acuff's development by letting him do basically whatever he wants. If we're simply naming the best rookie thus far this season, though, the answer is obviously Yaxel Lendeborg. Things have gotten harder with Stephen Curry sidelined, but Lendeborg has resuscitated Golden State's postseason ambitions. He's scoring efficiently, shouldering an enormous defensive load and has fit into a system that is notoriously tricky for the wrong kinds of players. Boozer may get there by the end of the season, but for now, this is Yaxel's trophy.

Salerno: In my rookie rankings released earlier this week, I had Yaxel Lendeborg No. 1. However, I would give strong consideration to Acuff because he is being asked to do more than any other rookie in his class. He is putting up elite numbers on a very bad Kings team that would be even worse if he wasn't in the lineup. I don't think you can go wrong with any of the top contenders. Darryn Peterson has also played very well as of late and will end up being in the mix down the stretch.

Botkin: So many good options here. Obviously the Grizzlies, who are probably the correct answer. I certainly didn't foresee Minnesota holding this tightly to the rope without Anthony Edwards. But I'm going with the 76ers, who felt like a team that was going to take a while to figure things out but instead are out to a 13-3 record. There are some qualifiers. A perfect 11-0 mark in clutch games is unsustainable, and they can't keep digging themselves into holes (six comeback wins from at least 10 down). But the bottom line is this is a team that looks like it has played together for far longer than it has. The roles clarified almost immediately. Joel Embiid hasn't gotten hurt yet. There's a mental toughness to this team that I suppose makes sense given the individual players we're talking about, but collectively this thing is way more tied together than I thought possible this early in the season.

Gonzalez: There weren't many people outside of Los Angeles who predicted the Lakers would be atop the Western Conference a month into the season. There might not have been that many inside Los Angeles either. The skepticism can be forgiven considering the Lakers bid goodbye to arguably the greatest player of all time during the summer, then overhauled a large portion of the roster. In came Walker Kessler, Quentin Grimes, Collin Sexton, Sandro Mamukelashvili and Matisse Thybulle, among others. After the reconstruction, head coach JJ Redick said that for the first time in his tenure "the pieces actually fit together." That's been the case so far on the offensive end. The Lakers are first in points per game and third in offensive rating. It definitely helps that Luka Dončić is playing some of the best basketball of his career and leading the league in scoring by a wide margin. While Dončić battles Victor Wembanyama for MVP frontrunner status, his Lakers are in a race with the Spurs for the top slot in the West. The former isn't much of a surprise, but the latter certainly is.

Kalland: Yes, the Grizzlies have faced a very generous schedule through the first month of the season, but even with that context, no one predicted a 12-4 start with Ty Jerome hanging out among the league's leading scorers. Cam Boozer's a strong ROY candidate (and is slowly improving his shooting efficiency) and the Grizzlies just keep finding diamonds in the rough to maintain competitiveness. They've got eight guys averaging 10+ points per game and are top 10 in offensive and defensive rating. Reality may arrive soon, but even so, this hot start has given them a great chance at emerging as a Play-In squad in the West.

Maloney: The NBA intellegencia was high on the Grizzlies coming into the season, but in the sense that they would surpass their win total projection and make a run at the Play-In Tournament. Instead, they've jumped out to a 12-4 start, which has them in fourth place in the Western Conference and is good for the fifth-best record in the league. They lead the league in offensive rating (121.2) and are third in net rating (+9.9) behind only the Spurs and the Celtics. Even though they've had the easiest schedule in the league thus far, this is still remarkable.

Quinn: For four games with Anthony Edwards, the Timberwolves looked like the NBA's best offense. Then their best player got hurt ... and they became the NBA's best defense. They're hardly slouching as scorers either. LaMelo Ball's playmaking has facilitated breakout years for Jaden McDaniels and Ayo Dosunmu. Jonathan Kuminga is making 3s and defending like the Warriors always wanted him to. Minnesota's transition from moodiness to giddiness is palpable whenever they play, and when they get Edwards back, they're going to be terrifying.

Salerno: Here is a wild stat for you: Cameron Boozer has a 159-21 record across games in high school, college and the NBA (during the first month of the season). He is the ultimate winner who elevates his respective teams to greater heights. Between Boozer being firmly in the Rookie of the Year race and Ty Jerome making a case as the Most Improved Player, the Grizzlies have been quite entertaining to watch. Memphis has pushed the right buttons.

Botkin: I'm probably a little biased on this one. I'm a lifelong Warriors fan and figured they would stink this year, but I allowed myself to get my hopes up with the way the team came out of the gate. I should've known better. As soon as Curry went down, which was probably inevitable, the Warriors turned into one of the worst teams in the league. It's a complete bummer. Hopefully he won't be out too much longer, and the Warriors can pick back up where he left off, but this is just a harsh reminder of how thin the margin is for this team, and it's just not likely to go their way over the long haul. If I was born in Indiana, I would say the same thing about Tyrese Haliburton's injury. Same goes for the Toronto fans with Kawhi only managing two games so far. All the injuries stink. But Curry's has hit the hardest.

Gonzalez: Moving to the 3-2-1 system was unnecessary. The league overcorrected for last year's perfect tanking storm and didn't account for a simple truth of basketball: sometimes teams are just bad. No amount of tinkering is going to stop that. More than half the teams in the East are under .500. The West has four more such teams, bringing the total league-wide to 12. Adam Silver didn't want to incentivize tanking, but by putting too much of the league's thumb on the scale, they've made it harder on the worst teams to get better. Not to mention that the odd entertainment value of fans checking their lottery odds in the tank wars sideshow has been somewhat stripped away. [Stands up and repeats himself yet again] Tanking wasn't actually a problem.

Kalland: The injuries so far this season have been brutal. Just about every team you'd point to as a disappointment -- Utah, Indiana, Toronto -- can point to injuries as a major reason for their early struggles. The frustrating thing is there's not an easy solve to the injury issue (schedule length is hard to blame for injuries in the first month) and every year it feels like we're playing injury roulette to determine who can and can't be a contender. The wheel started spinning earlier than usual in 2026-27.

Maloney: I'm going with Robby here. The absurd amount of injuries, coupled with who is getting injured, has been the story of the season so far. You could form an All-Star team with all of the guys who have gone down with multi-week ailments: Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren, Anthony Edwards, Tyrese Haliburton, Paolo Banchero, Kawhi Leonard, Stephen Curry, Austin Reaves, Dylan Harper, Jalen Duren, Lauri Markkanen, Jaren Jackson Jr., Kon Knueppel, Ja Morant, Caleb Wilson, Cason Wallace.

Quinn: Look, we knew Charlotte was taking a step back when the team traded LaMelo Ball. The Hornets have been plagued by injuries all season. Some of this can be explained. Fine. Their offense still makes me want to vomit. No team turns the ball over more often. No team shoots less efficiently. No team is forced to take more shots in the last four seconds of the shot clock. No team leaves you feeling as though you're watching a panicked 14-year-old try to play minutes for the varsity squad more often. I had very high hopes for No. 1 option Brandon Miller. I trusted the system Charles Lee built last season. I figured they'd be worse, but still respectable, because this organization has displayed a genuine, systemic competence over the past few years. I think that will win out in the end. For now, I pity the poor souls in Charlotte buying tickets to these games, because they're quite nearly unwatchable.

Salerno: Yes, Utah has been bad this season, largely due to the injury bug, but I was bullish on this team heading into the season. I had Utah finishing sixth in the West and making the playoffs outright. Instead, Utah is heading toward the lottery again, where it doesn't even own its own first-round pick in what should end up being a lackluster draft. The organization's top priority for the remainder of the season is developing Darryn Peterson.

Botkin: Spurs over Knicks. The Spurs are the clear Western Conference favorite with all the OKC injuries. The Wolves, Lakers and Rockets deserve to be in the conversation, but they're all second-paragraph entries. It's the Spurs until they get hit with some major injury, too, but let's not jinx it. In the East, I could make a case for four teams. The 76ers have the late-game goods and individual creation that is exponentially impactful in the postseason. The Celtics look incredible with Paul George flourishing. The Pistons are just flat-out tough and they've been doing it without Jalen Duren. But I'm still picking the Knicks, who are starting to come out of their fog. They are so perfectly built for the playoffs, and remember, they weren't a great regular-season team last year, either.

Gonzalez: Spurs over Celtics. After losing their first two games to start the season, the Spurs look every bit as good as they did during last season's run to the finals -- if not better. The three-guard starting unit hasn't slowed them down at all, and Wemby has been unreal at both ends of the floor. And while the Celtics took a lot of heat in the immediate aftermath of the Jaylen Brown for Paul George trade, we all should have known that they would still be among the best teams in the East this season. Both franchises are smart and steady. Meeting this summer would make for an excellent Finals.

Kalland: Spurs over Celtics. I have to stick with my preseason Finals prediction because it's not every year a preseason pick still looks that good a month in. The Spurs look like a juggernaut, and their top competitor in the West, the OKC Thunder, will once again (likely) be without Jalen Williams for the playoffs. We'll see what the Timberwolves look like when Anthony Edwards returns, but for now it still feels like San Antonio and everyone else. In the East, I felt good about this Celtics team entering the season, and nothing has changed my belief they have what it takes to win the conference.

Maloney: Spurs over Celtics. I picked Thunder over Celtics ahead of the season, in large part because of how difficult it has been for teams to get back to the Finals in consecutive seasons during this parity era. But now that the Thunder have been decimated with injuries, the Spurs have what appears to be a clear path through the West. I'll stick with the Celtics in the East, which has not been anywhere near as good as we expected this season.

Quinn: Spurs over Knicks. Oklahoma City's injuries are really all that's changed to me. I don't think the Lakers have the defense or frontcourt depth to win three straight series in the West. I don't think the Rockets will be able to create good enough shots. I need to see Ball prove it in a playoff setting before I trust Minnesota. The star-studded 76ers have thus far been clutch merchants. The underlying numbers are lower on them than their record suggests. The opposite is true for Boston, who is blowing everyone out of the gym, but is going to have issues creating shots off of the dribble in the playoffs and defending man-to-man against the best offenses. I have an eyebrow quirked at Indiana and Toronto when they get their best players back. I'll reengage with the Thunder if and when they cash in some of their trade chips. For now, though, nothing has convinced me that last year's finalists are going to be dethroned. The Knicks and Spurs are the most complete teams in their respective conferences, and I'd expect San Antonio to learn from last June's defeat in a revenge series this time around.

Salerno: 76ers over Timberwolves. Yes, I'm switching it up. I had the Thunder beating the 76ers in my preseason prediction, but I'm not sure OKC has enough firepower to make a deep run given their injuries. Minnesota is staying afloat even though Anthony Edwards is set to miss more time. LaMelo Ball has been fantastic this season. When Edwards gets back, I'm excited to see them play again. As for the East, it's really a toss-up to say who will make it out of the conference. Boston has been great. Detroit is playing good basketball. The Knicks and Heat are looking better. I still trust Philly's roster over all of them.

#2564. Jerry Jones calls Cowboys 'a bad team'; says team has chance to play better after Christian Parker's demotion

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eight teams have scored 26 or more points per game in the 2026 NFL season. The Buffalo Bills (31.9), the San Francisco 49ers (31.2), the Cincinnati Bengals (30.9), the Jacksonville Jaguars (29.9), the Dallas Cowboys (28.6), the Detroit Lions (28.6), the Chicago Bears (26.8), and the Kansas City Chiefs (26.3).

The Cowboys are the only team among those eight with more than two losses, and they have a 4-6 record. Dallas is one of only two teams with a scoring defense below league average, and theirs ranks 30th (28.2 points per game) out of the league's 32 teams. That's why Cowboys owner and general manager Jerry Jones felt comfortably calling his squad "a bad team" on Friday.

"We have not been a good team and are a bad team," Jones said Friday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas, via Yahoo Sports. "At 4-6, that says everything you need to say. ... Does that mean we will play a bad game [and] be a bad team on Sunday? Not necessarily. And that's why we're trying to improve."

One way the Cowboys tried to improve their ailing defense this week was to strip first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker of his play-calling duties and give them to senior defensive assistant Mike Pettine. However, Parker will stay on with the team to run defensive meetings and build out the game plans, but the 34-year-old, the youngest defensive coordinator in Cowboys history, will not have the play-calling role defensive coordinators usually have on game day.

"We've got a chance to play better doing it this way," Jones said of Dallas' demotion of Parker, via The Dallas Morning News.

After Dallas allowed the 49ers to rack up 584 total yards, the most allowed in a Cowboys' home game in the 67-season history of the franchise, they now have the NFL's worst total defense (393.8 total yards per game allowed), run defense (154.1 rushing yards per game allowed), third down defense (48.8% third down conversion rate allowed) and the worst defense in terms of defensive expected points added (EPA) per play (-0.13).

To be fair to Dallas' coaching staff, many of the defensive issues the last few years have been with the players on the field. Per CBS Sports Research, the Cowboys are the only team in NFL history to allow 27-plus points per game in three consecutive seasons with a different defensive coordinator each year: Mike Zimmer (2024), Matt Eberflus (2025) and now Parker (2026). Nothing has stuck, which likely has more to do with Jones' roster-building and decision to trade away All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons to the Green Bay Packers.

Jones' and head coach Brian Schottenheimer's handling of Parker is very weird, but the move could at least get Dallas to a 6-6 record after Thanksgiving. Dallas hosts the 1-8 Tennessee Titans in Week 11, then takes on the 2-7 Philadelphia Eagles on Thanksgiving Day.

An unusual MLB offseason is underway. The current Collective Bargaining Agreement is set to expire on Dec. 1, and MLB owners are expected to lock out the players. It will be the second MLB lockout in five years, and it will mean all transactions will come to a halt.

So what should we expect before the lockout begins at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1? Free agency is underway, and a few notable signings and trades have happened so far. The Yankees, for instance, agreed to a two-year deal with right-handed reliever Jonathan Loáisiga on Friday, bringing the pitcher back to the Bronx.

But we're still waiting on the first major move, and it could very well come before the end of the month. Tarik Skubal is the clear best player available on the market, an ace among aces who will play the entire season at age 30. The Mets, Blue Jays and Dodgers are seen as the frontrunners to sign the lefty, and he's recently started meeting with teams.

Behind him are lesser but still solid options in guys like Jazz Chisholm Jr., Tyler Rogers, Randy Arozarena and Freddy Peralta.

Sonny Gray (Twins), Evan Phillips (Braves), NLCS MVP Jake Bauers (Red Sox) and Dustin May (White Sox) have all also landed with new teams in November.

#2562. Meet Arjan Wijngaard, the man with 3,000 classic football kits in his possession

What do you do when you have nearly 3,000 football shirts in your possession? If your name is Arjan Wijngaard, the answer is allocate a room in your house as an exhibition space and log every single shirt in a comprehensive online catalogue.

Recently, These Football Times spoke to Dutch football shirt collector Arjan Wijngaard, the man behind www.voetbalshirts.org and the owner of one of the largest retro football shirt collections not just in the Netherlands but the whole of Europe.

For nearly 25 years, Arjan has been collecting football shirts from around the globe, beginning with an Everton shirt that was given to him as a gift in 1997. With such an enduring reputation, we asked him what drew him to collecting kits in the first place.

“The first question is the most difficult,” he says. “Of course, I liked football in the first place. That is an important thing if you want to collect football shirts. There is no particular reason why I chose shirts, though. Some people choose scarves (I have some scarves as well because if I can’t get a shirt when I visit a stadium or a game, I try to buy a scarf instead). Actually, maybe I’d better have chosen for scarves or pins; they are a lot cheaper and don’t need that much space!”

Take a wander into Arjan’s shirt showroom and it is easy to see what he means. From ceiling to floor, the walls are fitted racks that groan beneath the enormous weight of his collection. The door is an incongruous rectangle of white in an otherwise ubiquitous banquet of colour, while in the window two mannequins stand sentinel in green and blue raiment. It is a veritable sacrarium to shirts – from clubs both grand and meek.

“In general I like to collect shirts from clubs that are not very easy to find,” Arjan explains. “Like lower and non-league, for example, steps 9 and 10 of the [English football] pyramid or clubs from countries that are not known as famous football countries like New Zealand or Tanzania.”

Not that anyone can turn up and take a tour around his showroom, however. Arjan makes extensive use of the internet to display his collection, for he runs a website – wherein he catalogues the shirts by country, club and division – as well as Twitter, Facebook and Instagram accounts all under the banner of Voetbalshirts.org. But what inspired him to begin this online odyssey in the first place?

“There were a few reasons. Firstly, it is to show others what I have. Secondly, for the insurance to prove I had all the shirts if there is a fire or robbery. Also, having my collection online makes it easier for me to see what I’ve already got, especially when I am looking for new ones online and when I am in (fan) shops abroad.”

These are the two main avenues through which Arjan acquires the vast majority of his shirts. Prior to the ongoing global pandemic, he was undertaking around five trips a year to foreign countries in order to expand his collection, with two or three of these visits occurring across the North Sea in Britain. But with flight restrictions hampering his ability to obtain shirts from the clubs themselves, he has made increasing use of the internet.

“I prefer to get them personally from the club shop near the stadium, but that’s not always possible with over 2,700 shirts,” he admits. “Other options are online club shops and, of course, eBay but also groups on Facebook and other collectors here in the Netherlands, abroad and on Twitter. During the years, I have made some contacts all over the world and that is also a fun part of collecting.”

Indeed, Arjan is embedded deep in the football shirt community where he enjoys a prominent and active role as one of Europe’s most dedicated collectors. He presides over a football fiefdom of 6,000 followers across his three social media channels, while his website has attracted in excess of 200,000 visitors. But, he attests, the shirts themselves are not actually the most rewarding facet of being a collector.

“All the things that come with collecting are maybe even nicer than having the shirts. The visits to the stadiums, searching online, getting in contact with people, meeting other collectors and also volunteers that are proud of their club and want to help me to add a shirt or their club to the collection is great. Shirt collecting got me a lot of positive things besides the shirts themselves. Lots of talking about shirts and football and helping each other through our mutual passion of football shirts.”

As much as the community benefits are enjoyable, Arjan must have a favourite shirt, so we press him for an answer, hard as it may be to choose just one from 2,800 options. “There is one old FC Groningen shirt that is a favourite,” he admits at last, “because it is a rare one, matchworn and almost 40 years old.”

Such a rare and antique shirt is the pride of his collection and, like most of his garments, Arjan refuses to wear it for recreational purposes, although not necessarily for the reason most people might expect. “I tend not to wear my shirts because not all of the shirts are in my size (anymore)!” he says. “I don’t wear football shirts very often. I don’t want to damage them. But, actually, some I have double: one for the collection and one to wear.”

Even with such an extensive and valuable collection, Arjan still has his sights on expanding it further, even though his showroom appears to have reached the point of saturation. Even the door bears host to a number of caps hung on pegs hammered into the wood. He has a shortlist of kits he is working through and he reveals to us the one shirt he covets above all others.

“There is one shirt I really want to add to my collection, a matchworn Groningen cup final shirt from 2015. Groningen is my local team and they only won one trophy. The Dutch cup. And as I said before, I like shirts from non-league clubs I don’t have yet. So, if there are people who are reading this and think they can help me with a shirt from their local non-league club, don’t hesitate to contact me!”

Situated as he is in the Netherlands’ north-east, Arjan’s local team and the one he professes to support most keenly is Groningen, best known in recent years for being the boyhood club of Arjen Robben. It was a love affair that began around 30 years ago and which served as something of a gateway into his lifelong affinity for the sport and the kits associated with it.

“Groningen is my local team. I have had a season ticket for almost thirty years and the stadium is only ten minutes away by bike. My opinion is that you always have to support your local team. But Everton was my first shirt. I guess I like to support people’s clubs. Everton, Groningen and Feyenoord really are people’s clubs.”

Though the boom in shirt collecting has been a relatively recent phenomenon, and one which was no doubt exacerbated by a lockdown that allowed people to invest more time and money in starting or expanding their collections, Arjan has been active on Twitter since 2010. He is, for all intents and purposes, one of the old guard, but what does the future hold?

“I have no plans to stop!” he confesses. “As long as I like it and have the space to continue, I shan’t stop.”

#2561. Colts waive Daniel Jones: Indy not trading QB or Jonathan Taylor at deadline now a major second-guess

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Mobb Deep said it best: "Ain't no such thing as halfway crooks."

The Indianapolis Colts tried to sit on the fence at the 2026 trade deadline, ship away some (not all) expendable pieces, and land a somewhat respectable, middle-of-the-road record that might save a few jobs in the process. That meant moving on from the likes of DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson, and Josh Downs, but holding on to Jonathan Taylor and Daniel Jones. Less than two weeks removed from that semi-fire sale, it's safe to say Indy botched it.

What's the old saying? If you're going to be a bear, be a grizzly. Well, if the Colts felt alright selling some pieces at the deadline, they should've stripped it down to the studs, knowing full well they are entering a rebuild anyway after firing GM Chris Ballard in mid-October.

The losses have only continued to pile up for the Colts, which includes a demoralizing defeat at the hands of the Houston Texans in Week 11. That game, which dropped them to 3-8, proved to be the straw that broke the camel's back for the Daniel Jones era, as the team has since waived the veteran quarterback.

Again, this is a player who teams were reportedly interested in leading up to the deadline. Instead of pursuing those opportunities to shed a sunk-cost under center, ESPN reports that Indy rebuffed trade interest from teams like the Minnesota Vikings and Baltimore Ravens.

As a reminder, the Vikings traded a 2027 third-round pick to acquire Kirk Cousins, while the Ravens shipped a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 seventh-round pick to the Cardinals in exchange for Jacoby Brissett and a 2027 fifth-round pick. It's unclear what the compensation for Jones would've been, but I can tell you this—it's more than what they have now after waiving him: nothing.

In the nine games before the deadline, Jones had the Colts at 2-7 while completing 60.3% of his passes, averaging just 191.3 passing yards per game, and posting a passer rating of 68.9. In total, Jones had tallied seven touchdowns and 13 turnovers.

It was abundantly clear in the lead-up to the deadline that the two-year, $88 million extension the Colts signed Jones this offseason to was a disaster. Miraculously, a lifeboat drifted by them in the form of multiple teams inquiring about taking that burden off their hands, but they decided to stay on the deserted island. Now they're paying the price, with Jones set to account for $35.2 million in dead cap space for 2027 (provided he clears waivers) while the team pays him $49.8 million for 11 games played this season.

On top of Jones, Taylor, arguably the most sought-after prize on the trade market this cycle, should've been firmly on the block. With the Colts now without a clear answer at quarterback, Taylor is the living embodiment of that meme where the Lamborghini is sitting in the driveway of the trailer park.

He was most valuable to Indy as a trade chip at the deadline, and that remains the case this offseason. The only difference is that any team acquiring him is getting a back that's a little older, has a little more mileage, and doesn't help them for this stretch run in 2026. That sets up a possibly diminished return this offseason if/when the Colts deal him compared to what they could've gotten at this deadline.

For a team that won't have its first-round pick in 2027 after trading for Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline, they were in a position to refill the cupboard. Neither Jones nor Taylor likely would've fetched a first-rounder, but they would've given Indy premium ammunition for a later deal that could vault them back up. That level of asset mismanagement around the deadline now has the potential to ripple beyond just this second half of the season.

Jones being waived is just one of the initial steps that the Colts will take as they embark on this rebuild and they tripped out of the gate. Whether it's firing Shane Steichen, trading Taylor, or eventually hiring a new GM (if they can find a taker), the organization needs to have a more definitive and realistic plan for its future so they're not looking back with major second guesses like they currently are following this deadline.

#2560. Frankfurt’s pressing adjustments secure victory over Galatasaray – MH

von Next Generation am 22.09.2025 in den Kategorien Champions League mit 1 Kommentar

Eintracht Frankfurt won their opening Champions League matchday with a 5-1 victory over Galatasaray Istanbul. After about ten minutes, Frankfurt were trailing 0-1, but thanks in part to adjusted pressing, they were able to turn the game around. What follows is an aspect analysis of Frankfurt’s attacking press against the Istanbul side’s build-up play.

Frankfurt started, as usual, in a nominal 4-2-3-1. Ahead of the two midfielders Chaibi and Larsson, Uzun operated in the No. 10 role. On the left flank, winger Knauff played in front of left-back Brown. When dropping into a deeper defensive press, this structure shifted into a 4-4-2, with Burkardt and either Uzun or Knauff forming the first pressing line. In the transition to the attacking press, they shifted man-oriented as usual.

Galatasaray also began in a nominal 4-2-3-1. In possession, their structure changed depending on the depth of their build-up, forming something like a 3-2-5 or 4-2-4 through the positioning of the full-backs. Width on the right side was provided by winger Sané, and on the left by full-back Elmalı. Left winger Akgün frequently moved inside, acting as a kind of “free player.” Meanwhile, right-back Sallai tucked in slightly in higher possession phases to help form a back three in the build-up.

Galatasaray’s build-up was characterized by frequent rotations. Their basic reference point was the previously described 3-2-5. From this shape, they consistently sought positional interchanges in order to manipulate the opponent’s man-marking in the pressing phase. On the left side, Elmalı, who provided width, was able to vary his height. In deeper build-up phases, he often dropped further back, while he also regularly positioned himself on the last line. Winger Akgün was tasked with creating central overloads and repeatedly moved inside, at times even drifting over to the right side. In response to the full-back pushing high, the left holding midfielder, Lemina, rotated into the left-back position. Striker Yılmaz, in turn, shifted into the left half-space when the full-back stayed deeper and the winger dropped centrally.

Galatasaray’s left-sided rotations force Frankfurt’s pressing players into constant reorientation.

The purpose of these rotations was to manipulate man-marking and tie down specific Frankfurt players. Because winger Akgün frequently dropped into central areas, the two centre-backs, Koch and Theate, were occupied. Akgün positioned himself in front of striker Yılmaz in order to stretch the last line and create 1v1 opportunities. This produced a variety of different build-up structures, which required Frankfurt to constantly reorient themselves. For example, if Elmalı pushed high, he had to be tracked by Collins, and Galatasaray’s four attacking players tied down Frankfurt’s entire back line. This significantly complicated Frankfurt’s transition into man-marking, as the positioning of the forwards forced centre-back Theate to cover long distances during handovers.

Since all players in the back line are occupied, defensive handovers become more difficult.

Frankfurt’s plan, as in previous matches, was to shift into man-marking from a +1 overload through the handover of the opponents’ centre-backs and full-backs. The advantage of this approach is that spaces on and behind the last line can initially be secured, while the risk of a long ball leading to a 1v1 situation is minimized by having an additional covering player.

At the same time, after steering the opponent’s attack, the transition into man-marking could be executed to apply maximum pressure on the ball carrier. Depending on the opponent’s structure and build-up sequences, Frankfurt adapted their pressing schemes. For instance, they could vary the distance to their opponents during the pressing jump: larger distances allowed for greater security in coverage, while smaller distances created more immediate pressure.

Galatasaray tried to make these handover moments as difficult as possible for Frankfurt by forcing the distances at the moment of transition into man-marking to become as large as possible. The aforementioned rotations, for example, forced Theate into long runs to pick up winger Sané, so that Brown could then jump out to the still unmarked and deeper-positioned right-back of Galatasaray.

Because of Galatasaray’s attackers’ positioning, Theate and Brown are forced into long pressing runs. On top of that, Theate finds himself caught between two opponents due to the rotations.

Galatasaray also tried to open up the center through certain rotations, aiming to draw Frankfurt’s midfielders out of central areas. Frankfurt tracked man-to-man with Larsson on half-space player Gündogan and Uzun on the deeper right-sided pivot Torreira. Depending on the side of build-up, Chaibi was prepared to jump onto the more advanced pivot, Lemina. Because Lemina often rotated into the full-back position, Doan frequently picked him up, leaving Chaibi or Collins (depending on the movements of Akgün and Elmalı) unexpectedly without a direct opponent. At the same time, Gündogan and Torreira sometimes rotated in opposite directions, which created difficulties for Frankfurt in terms of handovers in central areas.

Because Frankfurt found it increasingly difficult to press Galatasaray’s build-up through their usual handover approach, from around the 15th minute they opted for tighter marking distances to transition more quickly into full man-marking. Brown pushed up directly, Theate went straight onto Sané, while Collins and Koch marked the two remaining forwards. This created a 3v3 situation on the last line. Although this increased the pressure on Galatasaray and led to more turnovers in their build-up, it also raised the risk against long balls due to isolated 1v1s. Time and again, Galatasaray managed to exploit this by sending strong dribblers like Sané into such spacious 1v1 situations. Even so, the tighter marking distances resulted in a much more balanced game with more frequent ball recoveries.

In the 30th minute, Frankfurt used a longer stoppage to make more significant pressing adjustments. Winger Knauff no longer pressed Galatasaray’s right centre-back but instead oriented himself toward full-back Sallai. This allowed Brown to stay on Sané, and Theate no longer had to make long runs out wide to cover him. At the same time, it was no longer problematic if all four defenders were tied up, as they no longer needed to jump out of the back line. The free centre-back was now primarily pressed by Uzun, who used his cover shadow to block passing lanes into pivot Torreira. Galatasaray’s build-up on the right side could then be pressed man-to-man through ball-oriented shifting. To this end, Chaibi stepped onto Uzun’s original opponent, Torreira, and the far-side Doan also moved into the ball-near center.

Frankfurt’s pressing adjustments: With no need to shift across the last line anymore, Frankfurt gains situationally much better access with less risk. These changes spark the turnaround in the match.

The pressing adjustments led to significantly better situational access and, at the same time, to much stronger defensive security. Frankfurt were able to use the resulting ball recoveries to establish longer possession phases, which gave them a more dominant style of play. One such spell of possession resulted in the 2-1 lead shortly before halftime. Immediately afterwards, a ball recovery from the adjusted attacking press led to a free kick, which in turn produced the 3-1 at the break.

In the opening 30 minutes, Galatasaray were able to cause Frankfurt problems, thanks in part to a very elusive build-up play that challenged Frankfurt’s typical pressing approach with its reliance on handover moments. Frankfurt’s adjustments, however, proved perfectly suited to applying pressure more easily while also improving defensive cover. The short interruption of play came at just the right time for Toppmöller and his coaching staff to implement the necessary measures. As a result, the pressing changes were decisive for Frankfurt’s eventual 5-1 victory and a successful start to their Champions League campaign.

Author: MH is a football aficionado at heart. His apartment resembles a football library, with shelves filled with books on the great tacticians from Rinus Michels to Pep Guardiola. #2559. MLB CBA negotiations timeline: League, MLBPA continue brawling over salary cap as Dec. 1 deadline nears

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As the 2026 Major League Baseball offseason continues to unfold, something vitally important to the future of the sport quietly hums in the background: the ongoing negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement.

The collective bargaining agreement, or CBA (or Basic Agreement, as it's known in a formal sense), is the negotiated accord between players and clubs -- i.e., the team owners and commissioner Rob Manfred, who represents their interests -- that governs the working relationship between the two parties, typically for a period of five years. It covers things as mundane as players' meal allowances and travel protocols and as vital as minimum salaries, the structure of free agency, revenue-sharing specifics, and roster sizes. Every CBA can be distilled down to a fight over money, or, more specifically, how the league's revenues will be divided between players and team owners.

The first CBA covered the 1968 and 1969 seasons and was the first in professional sports history. That was the handiwork of Marvin Miller, the pioneering head of the Players Association (i.e., the players union) and belated Hall of Famer. It was Miller's organizing skills, foresight, and training as a union economist that allowed him to make the Players Association a viable and effective labor organization. Every CBA negotiation from 1972 through 1994-95 resulted in some form and scale of labor stoppage, whether a players' strike or an owner-implemented lockout. After the cancellation of the 1994 World Series because of the worst labor stoppage in the sport's history, a long run of peace followed. That peace lasted until the prior CBA negotiations, which resulted in a 99-day lockout forced by team owners and delayed the start of the 2022 season.

The current CBA negotiations have been underway for some time, and not surprisingly, the two sides remain far apart on several key issues. The biggest fight will be over the owners' renewed desire to implement a salary cap, which the union continues to view as a non-starter. The push for a cap has less to do with the notions of competitive balance and more to do with the ownership's internal belief that being the only non-salary-capped league among the major North American sports is harming franchise values. The cap, though, is but one of many pressing issues on which players and owners must find congruity.

Moving forward, the process will be uncertain and rife with posturing and pointed public comments from both sides. The hope, though, is that a new CBA will be agreed to before the middle of March 2027, at which point there's a high risk of having the 2027 season delayed or even abbreviated.

To keep you informed of the twists and turns along the way to a new CBA, we've provided a detailed timeline of negotiations. That timeline will illuminate the important and finer points of the talks and, along the way, explain the implications of the various proposals coming from each side. The hope, of course, is that all of it culminates in a timely agreement that permits a fully intact and on-time 2027 season.

The MLBPA on Friday put forth a series of proposed changes to the international signing structure. Notably, the union did not propose the implementation of an international draft, which the league has long sought. "We are committed to negotiating a system that preserves opportunities for future generations of players, protects young prospects from exploitation, and provides flexibility without further burdening international players with new artificial restrictions like a draft," MLBPA interim leader Bruce Meyer said in a statement released by the union. "Our proposals help build upon baseball's advances as an international game, while safeguarding the interests of young athletes who are the future of our sport."

Specifically, the union's proposal calls for:

Also on Friday, MLB removed from the bargaining table an earlier proposal to exclude high school players from the annual MLB Draft. MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin said the following in a statement released by the league, which also includes a call for the implementation of an international draft:

"In recognition of the feedback we received from the MLBPA on our domestic amateur proposal, we made a concession today by withdrawing our proposal on high school eligibility and proposed to maintain the current entry rules for domestic amateurs. On the international system, we continue to believe it is long past time to reform the system in ways that would address longstanding challenges and benefit future players. The enhanced transparency of the International Draft that we have proposed best addresses the root causes of corruption in the current system."

Speaking to the media at the owners meetings in New York, MLB commissioner Rob Manfred said while there's room for compromise in general with the MLBPA, there's no room for compromise on the proposed cap and floor on team payrolls. "The owners want a deal with a salary cap and floor," he said.

"I can't imagine the owners ratifying a deal that does not include a cap and floor," Manfred also said. "... Thirty clubs are 100 percent unanimous in support of the proposals that have been made. I'm not in a position to speculate about what happens in the event that we don't achieve our overriding objective, which is to get a cap and floor system that addresses the competitive problem that our fans perceive."

MLBPA interim head Bruce Meyer, who has insisted that the union will never accept a salary cap, pushed back again.

"There can be no clearer example of the league's lack of seriousness than their insistence that they will not negotiate over the economics outside of a radical change to the system that would dramatically reduce overall player compensation for all categories of players and strip fundamental rights from players like the ability to have truly guaranteed contracts," he said Wednesday in a statement.

"There should be no illusions about the owners' true motivation in pushing for this system. They want to make more money in profits and franchise values by artificially suppressing player salaries."

To date, the league has tied every individual proposal to the players' acceptance of a cap-and-floor system. The players through their union have historically shown no willingness to discuss a cap on payrolls.

MLB Players Association executive director Bruce Meyer said MLB is not serious about preventing the lockout and has "wasted months of time" trying to court public opinion when the two sides could have been having substantive negotiations.

"At the end of the day, this is going to come down to the bargaining table," Meyer told the Boston Globe. "And we have been for months, since May, looking for a serious partner in negotiations, and the league has insisted since May that they won't negotiate over anything economic outside of our agreement to a salary cap. In that respect, we've wasted months of time when we could have been having a serious negotiation. So I'd say the more the league is focused on things other than bargaining with us in good faith, I would say that's counterproductive."

Meyer also said the MLBPA has put forth proposals intended to promote competitive balance and correct the game's revenue disparity, but the owners are focused on a salary cap to "increase their profits and franchise values." He added that the two sides have made progress on non-economic matters, such as drug testing and gambling policies.

To allow for a "smoother transition" to a salary cap/floor system, MLB proposed delaying its implementation until 2028. That would give teams time to prepare and get their payrolls in order, and allow for a full offseason heading into the system. The current competitive balance tax and revenue sharing system would remain in place in 2027.

"We recognize that clubs will need a full offseason to prepare to operate within the cap and floor system. Therefore, with this offseason already underway, we proposed today to begin the cap and floor system in 2028," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said in a statement. "This proposal would allow a smoother transition into the cap and floor system."

MLB also upped its salary cap/floor proposal to $258.3 million and $180.2 million, respectively. Back in June, the league proposed a $245.3 million cap and $171.2 million floor. It says it is willing to discuss further phase-in scenarios for a salary cap/floor system.

In its latest proposal, MLB proposed reducing the regular season from 162 games to 154 games, and adding a standard off day to every week. The league also proposed extending the Division Series from a best-of-five to a best-of-seven, and allowing higher seeded teams to select their opponents in the Wild Card Series and Division Series. As with every MLB proposal to date, the 154-game schedule and changes to the postseason format are contingent on the MLBPA accepting a salary car/floor system.

If labor strife lops off 60 or more games from the 2027 MLB season, then the consequences could be significant. The Athletic recently reported that if the forthcoming lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That's significant because commissioner Rob Manfred hopes to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. As such, this is a heavy incentive, at least on the league side, to not let any labor stoppage drag into June.

A poll of current MLB players across the full spectrum of salaries and service time conducted by ESPN showed strong resistance to the payroll cap and floor being demanded by ownership and league and being put forth as a precondition to every proposed change from that side. An excerpt:

How open are you to a salary cap?NL starting pitcher entering arbitration: Not open.

NL infielder making eight figures annually: Zero. No chance.

NL infielder on two-year contract: Zero. Absolute zero.

NL pre-arbitration journeyman: From what I've been told, I don't think it's good for the game. I just don't know if I know all the pros and cons of it. But, from everything we've been told, it doesn't sound like it's a good thing.

NL reliever on multiyear contract: With the right criteria, I'd be open to it.

AL starting pitcher in arbitration: I don't want it. In '94, they canceled the World Series, so if those guys can miss over half a year and miss the World Series, I think we're fully prepared to hold out for sure.

AL catcher entering arbitration: I need more information, but perhaps I would listen on it.

That's mostly strong sentiment that aligns with the MLBPA position on the cap, but it's not ironclad. MLB in negotiations and its public statements is seeking to tap into any existing divide between, broadly speaking, lower-salaried players with not much service time and more tenured veterans in their higher-earning years. There is a bit of a schism there, but it would take a substantial one to shift, in any exploitable way, the union's long-standing opposition to a cap-and-floor system. The ESPN piece covers an array of CBA topics. With the two questions related to the proposed cap, the responses can be broken down as 16 in mostly firm opposition to a cap and five not necessarily in favor but open to further discussions and reflection.

MLB proposed a series of changes to current roster rules that, in a statement, the league says are aimed at "creating more stability in rosters, getting the best players to the Major Leagues more quickly, and accelerating the pace of the offseason." Among the rule changes included in MLB's proposal are:

All the proposed roster rule changes are contingent on the MLB Players Association agreeing to a salary cap-and-floor system.

During a negotiating session with the league, the players' union puts forth its own proposed changes to the MLB Draft -- changes that are, in essence, a rejoinder to the drastic overhaul earlier put forward by MLB. Among the changes the MLBPA proposes are:

Additionally, the union proposes increasing the money payable to draftees under the incentive bonus plan and eliminating, according to the MLBPA, "the current practice of clubs deducting certain bonuses from players' continuing education benefits."

The timing of the draft has actually been a concern for front offices for years, since it was shifted later in the calendar to coincide with the All-Star break in 2021. Holding the draft in July crams both that and the trade deadline into just a few weeks and making it more difficult to allocate resources.

Commissioner Rob Manfred and interim union head Bruce Meyer each hold press conferences on the day of the All-Star Game in Philadelphia. "I think that I have an ownership group that is more united than any group in my entire time of baseball," Manfred says, referring at least obliquely to the league's push for a salary cap. "They are a group that believes in what I am arguing for."

"The supposed stewards of the game have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to convince those same fans that they don't have hope or they shouldn't have hope or that the product that they're paying to consume in record numbers is somehow broken," Meyer says of MLB's efforts to highlight perceived competitive-balance issues in the face of increasing attendance and television ratings. "I think it's perverse."

The MLBPA puts forth multiple proposals, many of them dealing with procedural matters for purposes of player health, safety, and wellness. They include:

The union's latest proposal is a reminder of the breadth of CBA discussions. Most issues are not the big-ticket items like a salary cap or lack thereof or revenue sharing structure but instead are somewhat esoteric matters that strike most fans as mundane. To players and teams, though, they're important considerations and in some instances may even provide a foundation of common ground moving forward.

More face-to-face negotiations take place, and MLB proposes more changes to the free-agency system, among other asks. MLB's latest proposal includes the following, all of which depend upon the union's acceptance of a payroll cap:

MLB in a prior proposal called for a cap on team payrolls of $245.3 million starting in 2027 and a payroll floor of $171.2 million. The league issues a statement that reads in full:

"The biggest issue baseball fans want solved to strengthen the game is fixing the payroll disparity that leaves too many fans without hope of their team competing for a World Series title. Every other major U.S. sport has tackled this problem, and every year more small market teams in those leagues have a chance to win. The salary cap and floor proposal levels the playing field, allowing us greater flexibility to address longstanding player priorities while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50/50.

"Today, in addition to proposing the largest ever increase in the minimum salary, earned by over half of MLB players, we accepted two landmark changes to free agency that have been in place for 50 years. We agreed to both the MLBPA's proposal to provide earlier access to free agency, and their proposal to eliminate the qualifying offer system, a provision players view as a drag on free agency. We also proposed to eliminate deferred compensation and to create a new 'Cornerstone Player' provision similar to the NBA's 'Bird Rights' to give every team a fair shot at retaining their fans' favorite star players.

"We will continue working with the MLBPA during the bargaining process to improve the game for teams, players and fans."

"After making a series of proposals to reduce player compensation by billions of dollars, eliminate fundamental rights with a salary cap, and destroy the amateur entry process, Major League Baseball and team owners are now attempting to distract from the true impact their plan would have on baseball. These misleading offers are designed to look like 'improvements' but are of little or no value, given they are expressly conditioned on agreement to the league's cap system which eliminates the free market, and ensures gains for one player only come at the expense of another.

"The league also introduced a litany of additional restrictions on player rights — limiting salaries, contract length, performance, award, and signing bonuses. While MLB claims to be acting in the interest of fans, their proposals thus far are entirely consistent with owners' long-held goals: suppressing player salaries and maximizing club profits.

"Owners' attempts to pit players against players are nothing new, but they've failed in the past and will fail again now, because PA members remain unified. We are committed to achieving a fair deal that protects the rights of all players, promotes competition, and leaves our game better for future generations."

Lacking from the league's latest proposal, at least on the public-facing side, is any revisiting of the recent changes to the draft and any mention of prior proposed changes to the league's revenue-sharing system.

During these same face-to-face sessions, the MLBPA proposes a ban on prop bets placed on individual players, ESPN reports. The idea is to preempt harrassment of players by gamblers. The proposed ban would extend to bets placed on individual player performance prior to and during any MLB game. The MLBPA also requested that players be permitted to engage in paid endorsements and sponsorships with sportsbooks and prediction markets.

MLB and the MLBPA meet for face-to-face negotiations, and owners propose sweeping changes to the draft and also push for an international draft. As for the MLB Draft, formally known as the First-Year Player Draft, MLB pushes for the following changes:

"Over the last several years, college baseball has undergone a remarkable transformation," MLB says in a statement. "Expanded scholarships, NIL opportunities, revenue sharing and significant investments in facilities and player development have made college baseball an increasingly important pathway that is producing major league-ready talent at an accelerated rate. Today's top programs provide players with resources, competition and national exposure that were unimaginable a decade ago. Our proposal is designed to build on that momentum to benefit the game at the college, minor-league and major-league levels. By creating a draft system centered around college-aged players and making most college players eligible one year earlier, more players will benefit from both a college education and an elite development environment while reaching professional baseball -- and ultimately the major leagues -- more quickly. We believe these changes will strengthen college baseball and deepen fans' connection to the next generation of major league stars. We look forward to working with the MLBPA throughout the bargaining process to modernize the domestic amateur system in a way that benefits players, clubs, and fans."

As for the international draft, MLB proposed making players outside of the U.S., Puerto Rico, and Canada (who are already included in the standard draft) subject to a similar system. The international draft would, as with the proposed changes to the MLB Draft, come with a $200 million bonus cap. At present, international amateurs may sign with any team under the international free agent system, although teams do have hard budget caps each year.

The MLBPA also issues a statement in response to MLB's proposals:

Today, MLB made another set of proposals that are flat out bad for baseball, ones that would cripple the next generation of players and damage the future of our game. They would, among other things:

Players remain committed to bargaining in good faith and leaving baseball better than they found it -- the league's proposals fall woefully short.

U.S. President Donald J. Trump publicly supports MLB's efforts to implement a salary cap. "If you don't have a salary cap, you don't have a sport, because they can't help themselves," Trump says. "Football has a salary cap. They should have done it a long time ago.

"It's shocking, frankly, that they didn't put a cap on many years ago," he said, possibly referencing the 1994-95 strike. "They had a chance to do a cap, but they blew it."

Speaking to reporters following the owners' quarterly meetings, Manfred addresses the luxury-tax system he and the owners seek to replace with a cap. "We have tried mightily over several rounds of bargaining to use a competitive balance (luxury) tax to address competitive concerns," Manfred says. "And sometimes you've got to admit you failed.

"We made a proposal on one set of topics. At the outset of negotiations, I went and said myself, 'We're open to whatever ideas people have, but we need a realistic framework that addresses the fans' concerns about competitive balance.' You just can't ignore that financial penalties have not gotten it done for us."

In a call with reporters, MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer addresses the owners' proposals. "Using MLB's definition of revenue and player share as set forth in their proposal and their presentation to us, player share under their proposal would go down," Meyer says. "Player share for this season, 2026, is projected to be well over 50 percent, using, again MLB's definitions of revenues and what counts against player share.

"Had MLB's proposal been in place in 2026, players, we estimate, would lose over half a billion dollars."

Meyer also refers to a salary cap as "a form of institutionalized collusion."

"Our salary cap-and-floor proposal addresses our fans' concerns by leveling the playing field while sharing baseball revenue with the players 50-50 like the other leagues," MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin responded on behalf of the league. "Under our proposal, major-league players will receive more compensation in year one of the system than in 2026. We are ready to listen if the MLBPA wants to counter our proposal at the bargaining table."

MLB and the owners publicly announce their first formal CBA proposal. Chiefly, they propose:

Using competitive balance tax (CBT), or luxury tax, payrolls as a guide, since they include benefits expenses, nine teams at present would be above the proposed cap line, while 12 teams would be below the floor. However, as Craig Goldstein points out, the amount needed to get all these teams below or above the relevant payroll thresholds amounts to an $18.7 million loss in aggregate player salary overall. Another sticking point will be how league revenues are defined. Owners no doubt seek to carve out things like real estate developments surrounding ballparks and ownership stakes in regional sports. As well, MLB's working definition of league revenues includes many expense deductions.

On another level, the fact that Manfred is able to persuade large-market, high-revenue clubs to agree to equal sharing of all local revenues is a notable development. However, such a concession by those large-market clubs may be contingent upon the implementation of a cap.

Another sticking point is that the league proposes an escrow system, as is used in the NBA and the NHL. This would mean a percentage of player salaries is withheld. If revenues fall short of projections, some of that money in escrow goes back to the league. If revenues are higher than projected, that excess is shared with the players. The MLBPA opposes the escrow system on the grounds that it undermines the notion of guaranteed player salaries.

The MLBPA makes an opening suite of proposals to the league, including:

"Today, the MLBPA (Major League Baseball Players Association) presented a comprehensive set of economic proposals designed to advance the rights and benefits of players at all levels," Meyer says in a statement released by the union. "Our goal is to preserve and improve baseball's market system, rewarding competition on and off the field. Additionally, the players' proposals provide increased revenue sharing initially guaranteeing every small market club a minimum of $240m in revenue every season. This enhanced revenue sharing includes added protections to ensure clubs prioritize winning over profiteering. Ultimately, our proposals are designed to build upon the incredible momentum and popularity of our sport world-wide."

"We appreciate the union making a set of proposals and we look forward to continuing the bargaining process and working towards solving the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us needs to be addressed," Caplin says in a statement. "We understand their proposals are designed to benefit players. Unfortunately, they do not address and in fact exacerbate the competitive balance problem our fans are telling us we must address. The MLBPA's proposal would reduce the amount transferred to lower-revenue Clubs, weaken the Competitive Balance Tax, and lead to even more payroll disparity than exists today. For example, under the Union's proposal, the Dodgers would pay less in luxury tax payments, giving them an additional $70 million to spend on payroll."

Negotiations on a new CBA formally begin between teams and players. Among the key issues to be discussed will be the league's desire for a salary cap, drastic changes to the revenue sharing system, league expansion, possible further playoff expansion, and an international draft.

The 2022-26 Basic Agreement is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET, at which point owners are expected to lock out the players in the absence of a new agreement.

#2558. NFL Week 11 injury report: Latest updates on Kenneth Walker III, Mike Evans, Baker Mayfield and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The regular season rolls on in the NFL with Week 11 already underway after the Houston Texans' victory over the Indianapolis Colts kicked things off on Thursday. Now, we have the rest of the slate on deck. While this is the smallest collection of games that we'll have this season (13) thanks to six teams being on a bye, it packs quite a punch. That includes a potential NFC Championship preview between the Vikings and 49ers in Mexico City.

Of course, as is the case with every week in the NFL, injuries are a substantial piece of the puzzle and remain a big storyline heading into each contest. This week, there are some heavy-hitters that headline the injury front. Namely, the Chiefs will once again be without star running back Kenneth Walker III, while Niners standout receiver Mike Evans (Achilles tendinitis) still has his status up in the air.

As teams across the league wrap up their week of practice, they've unveiled their final injury reports along with game statuses. Below, you can find updates for every game in Week 11.

Note: Atlanta, Cleveland, Green Bay, Los Angeles (Rams), New England, and Seattle are on the bye in Week 11.

Pinion nor Wayne was able to practice this week, so seeing them ruled out by Miami isn't too surprising. The Dolphins did get some encouraging progression from Trader, who was upgraded to a limited participant during Friday's practice. That gives him a chance, despite that doubtful designation. Each Dolphins player listed as questionable practiced fully on Friday.

Benford and Williams did not practice all week and have since been ruled out. Kincaid also did not practice at all this week as he deals with thumb and ankle injuries, but the Bills are holding out some hope by not ruling him out just yet, albeit listing him as doubtful.

After being limited on Wednesday and Thursday with a chest injury, Saints rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson was a full participant on Friday and carries no designation for Week 11.

Gordon did not practice at all this week for Chicago and has officially been ruled out. Meanwhile, Thomas popped up on the injury report on Friday as a non-participant due to an ankle injury that has him questionable.

Despite listing five players as questionable, the Titans are pretty healthy entering this matchup. Every one of those players was able to practice fully on Friday, which bodes well for their chances of being able to suit up on Sunday.

Outside linebacker Donovan Ezeiruaku was a full participant Friday and carries no injury designation for Week 11. This comes after he was a non-participant on Wednesday and a limited participant on Thursday due to an ankle injury. Safety Jalen Thompson was a full participant for the second-straight day.

Baker Mayfield is officially listed as questionable as the Bucs quarterback practiced in limited fashion on Thursday and Friday. Head coach Todd Bowles said Friday that Mayfield "had a good day today" and the team will continue to monitor him leading up to Sunday. If Mayfield cannot play, undrafted rookie free agent Jalon Daniels would start.

Mays did not practice at all this week for Detroit as he manages an ankle injury. As for the rest of the players listed as questionable, each practiced in a limited capacity all week. Meanwhile, safety Kerby Joseph is set to make his return after practicing fully all week and carries no designation.

Carson Beck did not practice on Friday as head coach Mike LaFleur noted the rookie is dealing with a back injury. As of now, the team is preparing for veteran Josh Johnson to start.

Kansas City will be without star running back Kenneth Walker III for the second straight week as he continues to deal with a groin injury. That'll thrust rookie back Emmett Johnson back in as the primary starter out of the backfield.

Every Steelers player listed with an injury designation, except Nick Herbig, was able to practice fully on Friday. That includes linebacker Patrick Queen, who was limited over the first two days of practice due to a hand injury. Meanwhile, Herbig did not practice at all this week.

Baun did not practice with the Eagles this week and has been ruled out due to a back injury. On a more positive front, wideout DeVonta Smith (hamstring) carries no injury designation, nor does running back Saquon Barkley (hamstring). Each practiced fully to wrap up the week.

Humphrey was sent home by the team this week and has been ruled out for this contest after he made disparaging remarks about the city of Baltimore on a podcast. On the injury front, Madubuike and Hawkins were unable to practice Friday and have been ruled out.

Okereke and Simmons were unable to practice this week and have subsequently been ruled out. Tight ends Tommy Tremble and Darren Waller are the only questionable players who were limited during Friday's practice (others were full participants). That marks the second straight day each was able to practice, albeit in a limited fashion, after missing Wednesday's opening session.

The most notable development on New York's injury report is who isn't on it. Geno Smith (ankle) has no injury designation after practicing fully on Friday, lining him up to start on Sunday.

Ladd McConkey has a chance to return to action this week after the Chargers wideout practiced in a limited fashion throughout the week amid a back injury. He's officially questionable.

Brock Bowers is officially listed as questionable as the tight end deals with an ankle and quad injury. Bowers did not practice on Wednesday, but was able to get on the field in a limited capacity on Thursday and Friday.

Denver is pretty healthy coming into the weekend. Lohner is ruled out, but practiced fully this week, while Jones was limited with a hamstring injury.

All eyes were on running back Bhayshul Tuten after he missed Thursday's practice with ankle and foot injuries. However, the back was able to return as a limited participant on Friday and carries no injury designation for Sunday's contest.

The Giants are extremely healthy entering Week 11, as no player was given a game designation.

Addison and Murray were unable to get on the practice field this week and have since been ruled out. Meanwhile, tight end T.J. Hockenson had been limited this week with a wrist injury, but was upgraded to a full participant on Friday and has no game designation.

The 49ers are hoping to have Mike Evans back in the lineup on Sunday in Mexico City as the veteran continues to deal with Achilles tendinitis. He's officially listed as questionable, and head coach Kyle Shanahan said the team will see how he is during Saturday's walkthrough before deciding his game status.
